review_text: Of all the ancient cities I visited in Sri Lanka, Polonnaruwa was definitely my favorite—even more than Anuradhapura. Although the entrance fee is a bit pricey for foreigners, it is absolutely worth every cent once you start exploring. The archaeological site is quite vast, so I highly recommend renting a bike or hiring a tuk-tuk driver for the day; it’s the best way to move between the ruins comfortably. What struck me the most was the atmosphere: at times, seeing the massive trees growing between and over the ancient temples reminded me so much of the vibe at Angkor Wat. It is a beautifully preserved window into history. Don't miss the Gal Vihara and the Vatadage—the detail in the stone carvings is incredible. A must-visit!

Highly recommended! Well preserved and impressive with its archaeological ruins, palaces, temples, stupas and Buddha statues. The last two tree pictures are something as cool as three trees living in symbiosis. Please rent a bike and book a guide. Becomes much smoother and more interesting.

Ancient main city of the island. Today only ruins spread over an area you have to travel by car , with guide or driver (extra charge) Admission is $30 per person to be transported from ruins to ruins with almost no information on the various monuments. At each stop "travelling merchants" insist on asking you for money, this makes the visit unpleasant in addition to lack of interest. Largely favour Sigirya The museum is pretty good

Polonnaruwa offers a captivating snapshot of medieval Sri Lankan civilization. The area boasts a dense concentration of ancient ruins, the centerpiece of which is the magnificent Vatadage, a circular relic house spanning 18 meters in diameter. This structure features breathtaking sculptural detail, including four beautifully preserved stone Buddha statues. Another key highlight is the Gal Viharaya, a rock temple renowned for its four antique Buddha statues meticulously carved into a large granite cliff face, each depicted in a unique posture. Visitors should observe a modest dress code when exploring these sacred sites: knees and shoulders must be covered. Given the humid climate, it is wise for those wearing shorts to pack a sarong to don before entering temple grounds. Additionally, be prepared to remove your shoes before entering the temple sites.

Starting in the morning from Dambulla and climbing Mount Sigiriya, we reached Polonnaruwa only in the afternoon, Hotel I did not book in advance, planning to stay in Polonnaruwa after all. However, the family did not want to explore the ruins of the ancient capital of the Sinhalese kingdom. All the more so they are at a decent distance from each other (e.g. lotus pool kilometers away from the museum).. So after leaving my wife and daughter in the cafe with my things, I headed towards the museum. The only free part of the complex is the ruins of Nishshankamalla Palace. It didn't take more than half an hour. If, unlike me, you want to explore the complex thoroughly, you need an entire day, a rental bike or a tuk-tuk with a driver and 25 USD.

A marvellous visit to this ancient city full of history of the early days in this beautiful island. A busy location and essential you have a guide to ensure you get the full benefit of the visit as the history is fascinating. Religious locations within the city to be acknowledged and respected ...... all in all a must visit if you are like minded and have a historical interest.

What a wonderful place. If you have experienced places such as Pompeii, Petra and Jeresh then you will truly appreciate this city. It is very spread out so consider how you will get around. Walking around the whole site is doable but impractical so consider hiring a bike, tuk tuk or even a car as you can drive between the main areas and park easily in designated car parks. Take water as it gets hot and also wear socks as much of the site is made up of temples so you must take off your shoes. If you are barefoot, the ground is very hot and socks will protect your feet. Remember for men and women that legs and shoulders need to be covered in the temple areas. This is a wonderful site with many beautiful remains of buildings with stunning architecture. Another tip...many of the buildings have multiple entrances so don't stand around for ages like everyone else trying to take a perfect selfie and getting in the way. Just walk to a different entrance which I promise you will probably more beautiful than where everyone normally stands.

Thoroughly enjoyed out tour through the ancient city. I would typically read my way through independently or use Google for info, but we decided to hire a local guide who was well worth it. Jayalath was very knowledgeable and gave us far more information than we would have thought to search for. There are many guides outside the ticket area but Jayalath was waiting at the first ruins area and gave us a much better rate. I would highly recommend finding Jayalath if you can and make the most of your trip through the ancient ruins.

I’ll open with I’ve been to a lot of ancient cities and a lot of temples over the years. Unless you’re a serious history/archaeology buff, this is probably going to be underwhelming. And even if you are, it will quite possibly still be underwhelming. The scale, taken as a whole is impressive, but it’s doesn’t really have that Angkor Wat wow factor plus the lack of information boards (some deliberately destroyed or defaced at that), maps etc for context, frankly useless guides and a high ticket price makes this a missable site from my perspective. We had a car and got through the lot in a couple of hours because to be frank, there wasn’t that much to see. The southern part of the site is in a poor state of preservation and this is exacerbated by a museum that may as well not exist and a disappointing amount of garbage. There are some standout parts of the northern part of the site, specifically Gal Viharaya which are very obviously well cared for. It’s a shame as it was obviously somewhere very important but precious little effort has been put into presenting the site. Don’t plan your trip around this - it’s a morning stop off at best.

The Polonnaruwa site is interesting to visit, but it covers several hectares and was extremely hot and heavy on the day of our visit. The entrance is, in my opinion, far too expensive for what it is, especially given the general condition of the site. The museum has no air conditioning, which makes it difficult to bear in high heat. Plan a cap, sunscreen and plenty of water!

Good half a day trip to visit the ancient city . There are about 5 stops you make as you move from the inner city all the way to the 3dd or 4th wall of the city with various temples and sites to visit . Good to know the context of these sites so would recommend a visit to the museum first to get a contextual understanding first before you see the significance of the ruins . The prices are relatively expensive but not as steep (pun intended ) as those in lion rock. It is atmospheric and Quieter than lion rock . Good to spend a couple of hours to three hours to visit .

The site is very large, consists of an introductory museum and then in the archaeological area there are 5 areas of major interest. To move between the different areas I recommend using the car with which you arrived, otherwise tuk yours, by bike or on foot but you need to evaluate that the distances are wide and with the sun it is very difficult. In the sacred areas you have to take off your shoes, your hat. Never photograph yourself turning your back on Buddhas. The site is very well maintained but the directions are scarce, better to be accompanied by a guide. Not to be missed.

Even this world heritage site is in a bit remote area for tourists, but it‘s worth putting this magic place on the travelling schedule. The remaining temples and buildings tell the story about the golden age from the second-oldest of all Sri Lanka's kingdoms. Rent a bicycle to cover the long distance between different parts.

There’s about 5 or 6 different sites and spread out over some distance so best to hire a driver who can take you from your hotel and around back, could be car or tuktuk, or there were some people on bikes. Lots of ruins to see but very exposed so considered the time of day, wear a hat, sunscreen, etc. Top tip: take socks to wear (as well as covering knees and shoulders out of respect) as you will need to remove shoes at some points but the ground will be hot / gravelly however socks are fine to wear and will make it more comfortable

After paying €26 for the ticket (in my opinion exaggerated for the offer - even in Italy I would not have spent these figures) we were not even given a map of the site (then sold at a high price by street vendors). Local guides stick to your ankles like mussels to parade you between $40-50 to accompany you on the visit. For me a criminal conspiracy, it's fine to profit on foreign tourists, but that's too much. The cute site, but there’s better in Sri Lanka

Such an amazing place to visit, well worth it, we had a guide who was able to explain all of the different areas. It was extremely busy with tourists and school children and was a much larger site than I realised it would be. A definite recommendation.

Fantastic experience, a must visit! So much extraordinary ancient ruins and monkeys. Definitely worth hiring a guide with a Tuktuk (available at entrance) who speaks good English, as they will tell you all the history and what each building was and what it looked like. Place is also very very big so need Tuktuk to drive around to see the best sites

Polonnaruwa is a fascinating ancient city full of history and impressive ruins. The well-preserved temples, statues, and royal palaces offer a glimpse into Sri Lanka’s rich past. A must-visit for anyone interested in culture, archaeology, or peaceful scenic walks.

The architecture here was beautiful and it was a great display of Sri Lankan history. We enjoyed the 4-5 hours we spent here and think it’s a great place to visit if you’re nearby. Between the ruins you can walk, cycle or drive. Although I would recommend driving in a tuk tuk, as it is cheap to hire someone to drive you and with the warm weather and long distance it is much easier than the alternative. The experience was very peaceful but I would recommend bringing some socks with you, as the ground is very hot underneath your feet!!! Overall had a great time here, however it was sad to see some tourists disrespecting the photography rules at Gal Vihara, so please ensure you are respectful during your visit!

We visited Polonnaruwa Ancient City, arranged by our private driver. For 20 € total, we got two entry tickets, two bikes, and a local guide who took us through the main historical sites. Exploring the ancient ruins by bike was such a nice experience and made it easy to cover more ground. Keep in mind that the full tour takes about 3–4 hours, and with the heat it can get pretty intense, so bring plenty of water, sunscreen, and a hat. Despite the weather, the history and architecture were absolutely worth it – a must-visit if you’re in the area.

You'll love this place of you love Heritage sites and have read into the history of Sri Lanka. It's quite peaceful but dont forget your socks and the stones can get very hot and you have to take off your shoes when walking around the temple ruins.

Archaeological and sacred sites spread over a large area. The bike OK but why not by car if you have your driver already booked. It’s hot and heavy, very little shade, especially in the sacred quadrilateral, despite the water, the hat, etc... The museum is very good, we can’t wait to be in the site, but finally a little disappointed, especially considering the price (I feel like all the national sites are at $35 per person now in Sri Lanka, which makes the trip overall expensive...). Gal Vidahar catches up with the impression, not to be missed of course if you go there

Several sites more or less rich on a huge surface: we thanked our guide who accompanies us on our road trip for transporting us from spot to spot: a few minutes of air conditioning in the van allows us to withstand a little better the sun of molten lead! The simple layman I am was impressed. The architects of the time, the masons, the sculptors made wonders.

A quick trip from the hotel was Polonnaruwa which was the Capital of Sri Lanka from the 11th to the 13th Centuries. It contains some splendid and spectacular statues. Plenty to see here and plenty to marvel about the history of this proud nation. A good tour guide will know the history of this place extremely well so tap into his knowledge. A must see

Polonnaruwa is a true gem for history lovers! The ancient ruins, giant Buddha statues, and serene surroundings made it a memorable trip. We rented bicycles to explore the large area—it was easy to get around and gave us time to enjoy the beautiful views. 📷 Booking was simple and entrance fees were reasonable for such a rich experience. There were no long wait times, and the site wasn’t crowded. Highly recommended for those who love history, photography, and peaceful escapes! 🛕✨

Most of the main ruins are located in one area, which makes it super convenient—you can explore them all using a single vehicle. The entrance ticket is just Rs. 60, and you can ask for a free map at the gate to help you navigate. We hired a guide for Rs. 3,000 to take us around the entire ancient city. Our tour began at the grand palace of King Parakramabahu and ended at the beautiful Thivanka Pilimageya. Parakrama Samudraya is also nearby, although it’s located slightly apart from the main ruins. On one side of the reservoir, you’ll find the palace of King Nissanka Malla. On the other side—not too close, but still easily reachable—is Pothgul Viharaya, where there’s a famous statue believed to be of King Parakramabahu and an ancient library.

An absolute must on a trip to Sri Lanka. Tickets are available at the museum for the equivalent of $30, are mandatory, without it is not possible, even if you often read about them on the net. You can also buy them online beforehand, but there was no queue, credit card is accepted, at least Visa. There are various checkpoints for tickets! At the museum you are approached directly by the guides - who suggest a guided tour with TukTuk for an average of 25$ - significantly too much (untypical for the country with an average daily earnings of 10-15$) for the 2-3 hours. We used the TukTuk service without a guide for about 10$. On foot not feasible the whole thing. The driver drives you to all the highlights, briefly explains the most important one, then you walk alone and then you go to the next spot...

If you have better guidance, as there are many interesting corners, some well preserved and others are just ruins. It's a great display of the island's history. You have to take the tickets at the ticket office and hand them over one by one in the different tickets. Especially that they do not keep any, they just have to chop or tear a piece, we had problems in a ticket because we were missing one that stayed in the locker, and they do not attend to reasons, good thing we had driver and helped us. Gal Vihara is a must visit with shows different forms of Buddha. Don't miss to spot green coloured nails of statue. A must visit place in Srilanka.

Polonnaruwa is an absolute gem for history enthusiasts and anyone fascinated by ancient civilizations. As a UNESCO World Heritage site, it offers a remarkable journey back to the 10th and 11th centuries when this city was the thriving capital of Sri Lanka. The ruins here are incredibly well-preserved, allowing visitors to truly imagine the grandeur of the ancient kingdom. The intricately carved statues, stupas, and temples scattered across the site are breathtaking. Highlights include the Gal Vihara, with its stunning Buddha statues carved out of solid rock, and the Royal Palace, which gives a sense of the architectural splendor of the time. What I found particularly captivating was the sense of tranquility that envelops the entire area. Despite being a popular tourist destination, Polonnaruwa never feels overcrowded, allowing you to explore the ruins at your own pace. Cycling around the site is a popular option and adds a bit of adventure to the experience. Make sure to visit the Archaeological Museum before heading out to the ruins. It provides valuable context and enriches your understanding of the site. Overall, Polonnaruwa is a must-visit for anyone traveling to Sri Lanka. It offers a perfect blend of history, culture, and natural beauty, making it an unforgettable experience. Don’t forget to carry water, a hat, and sunscreen, as the sun can be quite intense, especially during the midday hours.

We stopped off on our way between Sigiriya and Passakudah and spent a few hours exploring this historical place. This is a ‘do not miss’ experience. The ruins of this huge ancient city provide a fascinating insight into the sophisticated skills and technology of the Sri Lankan people hundreds of years ago. The palace, sacred places of worship and huge carved images of the Lord Buddha are incredible but all around there are also the ruins of many ordinary houses and shops. The ruins cover a vast area. Many people hire bikes and pedal their way around which looked like hard work in the heat. Instead our driver drove us from site to site and we also hired a guide ($40) when we arrived at the ticket office to tell us all about the history which really added to the experience. There are many hawkers trying to sell souvenirs, drinks etc. They’re a bit annoying but I guess are just trying to make a living so just be patient.

Interesting archaeological area, composed of several sites (fortress, palace, various temples, ponds, etc.) that integrated the city that bore that name. It is advisable not to do it exclusively on foot, because the places to visit are sometimes relatively far from each other, and the heat can be very overwhelming. We did it by car, but there were tuk tuks everywhere to make the tour easier. It is worth it, especially the temple of the three Buddhas, which has spectacular sculptures.

the royal city itself is beautiful and you must have seen it, but be careful if you take a guide. we had a guide with tuktuk from the park he asked 60 euros for 3 hours to show the city when he was done for 1.5 hours and I gave him half he got angry and threatened. So be careful who you take especially when the entrance fee is 35 dollars per person.

The site itself is very large, and full of some incredibly interesting history, and impressive sculptural edifices. However, the entrance fee is somewhat steep (US$30), and the guides don’t - in our experience - add anything whatsoever to things. Ok, so taking a guide is optional but we hoped that, being novices in Sri Lankan history, we might get a lot from one. So, when one jumped on us as soon as we pulled into the car park, we agreed on a price to pay if we appreciated what he had to tell us, and another if not. Sadly, we quickly realised that he had simply memorised what is detailed on the metal plaques at the entrance to each site, and couldn’t answer any of our questions, preferring to repeat what he had just said. That undoubtedly clouded our overall appreciation of the visit, and we would have been better relying on a good guide book. We’d definitely recommend hiring bikes to get around the site - it’s very straightforward to do, and they can be hired for around US$3-5 per person. Overall, a fascinating site to discover, if done in the right way.

At $30 per head and no family discount, it is very pricy for what is on offer.  Mostly empty ruins with little inside them.  Go in the evening to avoid mid-day heat (these are all open-plan and exposed).  Use a driver to talk you from sight to sight.   Takes about 3 hours max to see everything.

We visited this ancient site one morning in August, accompanied by a guide. The city incorporates palaces, monasteries and Buddhist and Hindu temples. It is a fascinating insight into Sri Lankan history & the archeological remains are relatively well preserved. You’ll also get to see an abundance of monkeys such as macaques and the more elusive purple-faced leaf monkey. Well worth a visit. Expect to spend half a day here.

Polonnaruwa is a captivating journey into Sri Lanka’s ancient past, and guiding visitors through this remarkable UNESCO World Heritage site is always a rewarding experience. As a tour guide, I’m continually impressed by the grandeur and historical significance of Polonnaruwa, which stands as a testament to the island's rich cultural heritage. The city’s well-preserved ruins offer a fascinating glimpse into the medieval era of Sri Lankan history. From the majestic Royal Palace to the intricate carvings of the Gal Vihara, every corner of Polonnaruwa tells a story of a once-thriving capital. The architectural beauty and scale of these ancient structures are nothing short of awe-inspiring. One of the highlights for many visitors is the chance to explore the Parakrama Samudra, an extensive irrigation system built by King Parakramabahu I. The sheer scale and ingenuity of this ancient engineering feat provide a fascinating insight into the advanced technology of the time. Walking through the ancient streets of Polonnaruwa, I love sharing the historical context and legends that bring the site to life. The blend of ancient temples, royal palaces, and elaborate stone carvings creates a rich tapestry of Sri Lankan history and artistry. For anyone interested in exploring Sri Lanka’s cultural heritage, Polonnaruwa is an absolute must-visit. Its historical significance, architectural marvels, and serene setting make it a memorable experience for all. Join us on a tour and immerse yourself in the fascinating history and beauty of this ancient city.

The vast archaeological site corresponds to what has been unearthed so far in Sri Lanka's second capital at the end of 900 AD. In addition to the amazing and huge Brahmin monuments,.you can admire what remains of the beautiful palace-garden (and the water pipe systems. These numerous and often well-preserved remains are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The ticket office is across the street from the entrance to the site. There are numerous exhibits but it is not very eye-catching and sometimes the meaning of the exhibition is not even clear. Museum and the 5 focal points of the archaeological site are quite far away, considering the hot weather. A guide with tuktuk costs about 5000 rupees (negotiable) but it's worth it! We, being 4, were able to follow it with our mopeds. Last but not least, the admission price is absolutely disproportionate; $30 per person, without discounts for students, seniors, families, only for children. That said, if you have to choose to neglect a site between Polonnaruwa, Sigirya and Danbulla, skip Polonnaruwa.

For people who are used to traveling, the site is not exceptional. At $30 entrance, this archaeological site of 122 hectares is not up to the price compared to other monuments in Asia or elsewhere (Angkor $37, Hampi in India $17, Petra $58 over 2 days...) Even if the bike ride of more than 3 hours was very nice and the site rather well maintained, this site remains interesting but overrated.

Great ruins but appalling signage and no explanation concerning where to go. Quite a lot of money to spend for a site which clearly has had no maintenance or proper management for a long while. Be prepared to be plagued by hawkers at every turn throughout your visit.  The ruins themselves are impressive and worth a visit despite these setbacks

I highly recommend it. Not only is it atmospheric and interesting from the point of view of historical heritage and architecture, but you can also just walk around beautiful places - green everywhere, monkeys, deer, monitor lizards, colorful birds. It’s a huge area; I recommend moving between locations by car or tuk-tuk. There is also an option on bicycles, but this is for winter; in summer it will be very hot. We walked there 8 km, taking into account the fact that we were by car. Don't rush, you can see a lot of interesting things in the details, for example, in the pillars of the Atadage temple)) However, my favorite there is the temple of the image of Buddha Lankatilaka. Tickets with three tear-off coupons are purchased at the archaeological museum (as of June 2024, $30 for adults and 15 children). Clothing is standard for Buddhist temples - covered shoulders and knees, shoes will need to be removed. You can take socks with you, the stones are hot. All places are marked with signs with descriptions in English, Sinhala and Tamil. We studied the information in advance; there is no point in taking a guide. Few people will tell you better than what is written on the Internet, and especially in Russian. Of the minuses - the traders are insanely annoying in each of the locations

I read a lot of negative reviews of the Polonnaruwa ancient site, and I am a little surprised.  I can only assume that because people don’t make good choices with their planning, they end up not having a nice time. The two things that we did right to ensure a good experience were….start early- as soon as the ticket booth opens - you will get the least crowds, the best light and the coolest weather (relatively)…….the second thing is to do it by tuk tuk….it is a large site and trying to visit by cycling or walking will only make you hot, tired and miserable, this leads to the travel state known as “everything sucks!”. My wife and I spent a long half day morning doing the following: Firstly we purchased the Polonnaruwa Ancient Site entry tickets at the Archaeological Museum in Polonnaruwa. The address is WXRX+PFG in Polonnaruwa It cost US$25pp. They take credit card or cash is accepted. There is a ticket office for locals and separate ticket office for tourists which is a bit further down the path on the right. Tourists can also buy online at the official website of sigiriyafortress. The entry ticket is for 3 areas, and as you visit each area they tear off a stub for each one as you enter that particular part. Near the ticket office is where local guides canvass the tourists. Unfortunately we got ripped off and paid too much. The going rate is US$20. The guide jumps in your car with you to move from one site to another. At the end he gets a tuk tuk back home. The guide that hooked us claimed to be an archaeologist who had worked on these ruins. He separated us from our private driver so he could puff up a guiding fee from the usual US$20 to US35. We later found out he was going to share the extra money he conned off us with our driver but our driver told him to just charge us the usual US$20 fee instead. Seems our driver had been duped also. We then went to the Statue of Parakramabahu I (Pothgul Vehera statue) which is located on Bund Road to the north of Polonnaruwa, on eastern bank of Parakrama Samudraa reservoir. It is 100 metres north of the ancient Potgul Vehera monastery. This is free to enter so not part of the entry ticket. Next we went to Dalada Maluva  which is the Sacred Quadrangle. This has: - Vatadage Polonnaruwa which is a circular relic house and well preserved - Nissanka Latha Mandapaya that is a pillared structure that is open on all sides - Gal Potha stone inscription is a Stone Book  that is lose between the eastern outer wall of Hetadage and Sathmahal Prasada. Unless you know what it is this stone book could be easily missed even though it is huge. - Hetadage which is sometimes spelt Hatadage is an ancient relic shrine. Note that for some of these ruins you are required to remove shoes but it well sign posted. Next we went to Gal Vihara aka Uttararama which is impressive with various Buddha’s carved in a stone wall made of giant granite. One is a reclining Buddha carved into the side of a rock face. The entry fee is included in the Polonnaruwa Ancient Site entry tickets. Visitors need to cover knees and shoulders and has guards checking this. Next we went to Lankathilaka Image House which is a big standing 17meter high Buddha. Second last was Thivanka Image House that is located on Thivanka Pilimage Road in Nissankamallapura. The fee is included in Polonnaruwa entry ticket. Lastly we went to the Lotus Pond (Polonnaruwa Nelum pokuna) that is located 400 metres south of Thivanka Image House. There is a lot more ruins in all these areas but we tried to see the highlights that intersted us.

The area ruled Sri Lanka from the 11th through 13th centuries. Several buildings here likely held the Tooth Relic. There are other unique structures like the circular Vatadage and the oddly shaped Satmahal Prasada, the purpose of the latter unclear. Places like the Lankatilaka Vihara, stretching to the heavens, will catch any photographer's eye. The sublime sculptures at Gal Vihara represent the best of Sinhalese craftsmanship, the artistry of the Kumara Pokuna, the royal baths, not far behind. It is not a large area and the ruins aren’t as intact as in Angkor Wat, if a comparison needs to be made. But it is a good introduction to the history of Sri Lanka. The second most ancient of Sri Lanka's kingdoms, Polonnaruwa was first established by the Chola dynasty after their successful invasion of the country's then capital, Anuradhapura, in the 10th century. The Ancient City of Polonnaruwa has been declared a World Heritage Site. Polonnaruwa is the second largest city in North Central Province, but it is known as one of the cleanest and more beautiful cities in the country. Polonnaruwa was ruled by the Kings Vijayabahu I, Parakramabahu the Great and Nissanka Malla – all 3 of these rulers devoted themselves to fostering agriculture, religion and social development and the kingdom prospered under their reign during this era.

From the museum to the many sites throughout the ancient city, Polonnaruwa was probably our favourite stop in the Cultural Triangle. Not as old as Anuradhapura, or as well preserved, it is better organized and you can more easily develop an understanding of the different eras and constructions. You’ll need a few hours to see it all, but you’ll want to spend time checking out the different sections and appreciate the artistry evident in many of the ruins. The only drawback are the numerous, persistent vendors at nearly every stop (something that isn’t condoned at Anuradhapura), but be firm, polite and keep moving and they will leave you be (eventually).

After touring we took a lunch in The Lake House, which is so nice place for a rest. It was a pleasure to go around with my guide and work out what everything was and try to imagine how everything would have looked in the past. This archaeological site is extensive: impressive ruins, remnants of ramparts, sunken gardens, remains of temples, the Royal palace and Council Chambers, stupas, impressive tombs of varying size, a monastic hospital  site, and many steps. The site covers 35ha. and is the largest monastery complex in Polonnaruwa. Parts of the Lankatilaka Vihara still stand; two 17m high walls, each 4m thickness and adorned with impressive murals, form an aisle to a headless 14m high Buddha statue in this ancient temple. We had the services of a terrific guide, he had an encyclopedic knowledge of each structure and ruin and made our visit a rich and rewarding experience.

This is one of the ancient capitals of Sri Lanka, centuries old and with a number of sites contained therein. Entry is USD 25 for foreigners and USD 12.5 for children (half rate for nationals of SAARC countries). Payment can be made in USD or LKR, but change is returned in LKR only. Paying in USD is every so slightly cheaper when you do the reverse forex rate calculations. Upon paying the entry fee, you can enter the area and see all the various attractions. There is not a lot of information available on-site, so hiring a guide can be worthwhile. There is a museum in the building where you buy tickets, entry to which is complimentary with the Polonnaruwa tickets. However if running short of time, can skip this (which is what we did). Since there are around 26 sites within the premises (all spread apart), it can easily take upwards of 1 whole day to see the place in its entirety and enjoy its beauty. If running short of time, you need to plan in advance and shortlist the places you want to see and first finish those (and then, time permitting see as much of the rest as possible). The Golden Quadrangle, Palace Complex and Gul Vihara are some of the places that i would recommend as must-see. Suggest carrying a lot of water, wearing hats and covering knees. As with most historic ruins, children and people without a sense of history will find this dull, so i would suggest they opt out (instead of paying 25 USD and then realising that they didnt appreciate the beauty of the ruins).

I would not hesitate to name Polonnaruwa as one of the best 10 cities to visit in Sri Lanka. I would also say that it is immaterial whether you are a local tourist or an international tourist. I must also say that, over the years the city is becoming increasingly tourist friendly. About 10 years ago when I used visit here there was hardly any decent restaurant or a place to stay. During the last 4-5 years a large number of such places have been built - and more are being commissioned. Road widening and landscaping is still going on (March 2019). In a few years time I would expect a marvelous city here. This is beside the old glory of Polonnaruwa that was always a great tourist attraction. The pick of the sites is Gal Vihara inside the historic city that you can enter by purchasing passes. The majestic Buddha statue in Gal Vihara is an overriding reason for me to visit the place again and again. There are many other monuments inside the historic city that a tourist should not miss. Apart from the historic city one should make it a point to visit the Parakrama Samudra (sea of Parakrama) - a sizeable reservoir built by the king Parakramabahu and later expanded by the first Prime Minister of Sri Lanka, D S Senanayake. It's possible to take a boat ride (no motor boats) in the lake which is highly recommended for the birders and bird photographers. There are a few islands in the lake that are are inhabited by many species of water birds. The bank of the reservoir is a great place to photograph birds flying to and from the islands in the morning and evening. Adjacent to the bank of the lake is the museum - a must visit place. In future, the museum may be relocated in a more spacious modern building in New Town, though. Polonnaruwa is still a city unaffected by the plague of vehicular traffic as do many other cities in Sri Lanka. Enjoy driving /riding in this picturesque city before it is too late!

Polonnaruwa is a well maintained and well enough run ancient city/archaeological site in the cultural triangle. Its very easy to get around via tuk tuk (and fairly inexpensive too) or you can go the bike route if you don't mind the heat. There are a number of sites to see but it can all be done in about three hours if you have a tuk tuk. Visitors should be prepared for crowds of people, many of whom will ignore well placed and easy to read signs about taking off shoes and not climbing on crumbling walls. There will be people in all of your pictures as well. Ultimately I have two different recommendations re: whether to visit: (1) If you have never seen a similar site I would recommend going - you will be interested the whole way through. (2) If you have been to  multiple other sites as I have, including in Cambodia, throughout Thailand and Burma this is ok to skip. I grew bored pretty quickly and didn't see anything new/different that made it worth a special trip. If you are in the area with an afternoon to kill (as I was) there are way worse ways to spend your time but be prepared to be underwhelmed.

The world heritage ruins at Polonnaruwa appear to be on the list of every tour that passes through Sri Lanka's cultural triangle.  We were staying locally so could get a head start on most of the tours before they poured in.  Most people seem to cycle around the ruins and I could see why this would be attractive - it's cheap, easy and safe, and you can move between the different sites fairly quickly.  However, we were advised by a local to head to the top of the site by tuktuk then walk back to town, and I'd highly recommend this approach too - you'll get to see a lot more wildlife when you're walking, and trust me there's a lot to see if you keep your eyes open!  Saying that, you'll probably be fairly tired by the end, and make sure you take plenty of water.  The ruins comprise of a number of main sites interspersed by smaller, less-visited sites.  Be prepared for crowds at the main sites, with far fewer tourists at the smaller ones.  All are worth a visit though.  OK, this is not Angkor or Bagan, so don't expect it to be - I've been to both those and still reckon this is worth a visit if you're up in the cultural triangle.  However, I wouldn't bother staying in Polonnaruwa, I'd probably stay somewhere else - such as Dambulla - and get a tuktuk across for the day.

If this is the first Buddhist archaeological site you've ever visited, I'm sure it will be fine. Well maintained grounds, decent infrastructure for bike and tuk-tuk tours, and surprisingly good signage in English for this type of site. ...but if you've done any of the other Theravada Buddhist sites in Asia, this will leave you wanting more. Having done Bagan, Angkor, and Ayutthaya, I found Polonnaruwa downright boring. Granted, I'm jaded at this point, but I can't recall anything at this site that I hadn't seen elsewhere--other than the big temple that is positively *vibrating* with a bat colony in its hollows. The site also has that Angkor-esque picture taking issue, where the entire grounds tends to be distilled down to only a few scenic venues when people are showing off this place in pictures. I.e. if you're thinking of going based on a well-balanced shot of a seated Buddha surrounded by broken columns, be aware that you're not going to enter a site replete with similar ruins: you're seeing a picture of the only kneeling Buddha at Polonnaruwa surround by broken columns, and any pictures you get are going to exactly resemble the postcard that pulled you to Polonnaruwa in the first place, leaving one to wonder exactly how unique an experience it actually it to visit Polonnaruwa at all.

Once an ancient capital of Sri Lanka, Polonnaruwa is a must-see on any visit to this beautiful island.  The site itself is vast, with lots of ruins of ancient stupas, temples, water gardens, monk's lodgings, moats, etc  dotted around. it must have looked somewhat like Angkor Wat in its heyday. It is also hauntingly beautiful now, and although one of the more popular tourist sites, never seems crowded because of its vast size.  Towards the end of the site are exceptional and magnificent representations of the Buddha carved in stone - standing, seated and laying down. Definitely not to be missed!... For me however, the most intriguing building of all at this ancient site is a very odd and out- of- place (i.e.not buddhist nor hindu ) temple that has puzzled even eminent archaeologists which bears remarkable similarity to the architecture of the pyramids of the ancient Maya.  How can that be possible?......  A real mystery!

Polonnaruwa as you may be able to see the site scenes of Ancient city which can be considered as a Kingdom well run or managed with improved ways of irrigation, cultivation and the ruins denotes the spacious living of Kings with loads of entertainment in an Environmentally friendly way which is not possible now a days. One can understand the level of Engineering. Socks are recommended when entering the temples as it can be very hot underfoot. About half way round there are toilets – those for foreigners were clean & in a reasonably good condition. There were also the aforemen-tioned refreshment stalls. There are similar facilities (albeit less clean toilets) just before the exit. Don’t forget sun cream, water, and bear in mind the need to cover shoulders and knees. No sleeveless shirts or shorts.

We spent an enjoyable few hours exploring this ancient site.  We were on a bit of a tight time deadline and were torn between Polonnaruwa or Anuradhapuda, am glad we chose the former as it's a fairly compact, self contained site, with good access to all the ruins.  Yes it's not as glamorous as other countries' ancient sites, but it is of great historical and cultural significance in Sri Lanka and several of the buildings are well preserved to say they were buried beneath jungle for centuries! There is ample parking and good visitor facilities (toilets, wash facilities, food and drink) We travelled around by car, which was straightforward enough.  There are several services hiring out push bikes, which seemed a pleasant way of getting around. We had a very informative guide book, which we used to navigate and inform our route round.  There are some information boards dotted around, but they don't give particularly detailed descriptions.  As with any historic site visit, there are several 'guides' hanging around offering their services, if you are without a guidebook and find a good guide I would recommend it as you will miss out on a lot of information and even miss some of the well hidden sites altogether! You do need to remove headwear and footwear to enter a large number of the sites, so come prepared and maybe bring something to dust the gravel off your feet after. I would highly recommend a visit here during a tour of Sri Lanka's 'cultural triangle'.

As I was staying in Dambulla, I had to take a bus to visit Polonnaruwa’s sights. From the main street of Dambulla, there are regular buses heading towards Kaduruwela – which is an adjacent part of Polonnaruwa where the train and bus stations are located. Hopping onto any bus that is heading to Kaduruwela will get you into Polonnaruwa. However, it is best to tell the bus conductor to drop you off in the “Old Town”, which is (I think) the first main drop-off as you enter Polonnaruwa (from the direction of Dambulla). The bus journey took about 90 – 100 minutes, and cost 100 rupees. After getting off the bus in the Old Town, ask around to get to the Museum -- just short walk away along a canal -- where you can buy a combined ticket for the museum and the archaeological sights. It cost 3975 rupees but is valid only for one day. The museum gives a so-so introduction to the history of the Sri Lankan kingdoms, putting the ruins of Polonnaruwa into a larger context. Curation has room for improvement. Moreover, the airconditioning was weak and it was warm and humid inside the place. The ticket comes with a pretty useless map. The staff know that the map is useless. So the lady advised me to take a photo of the wall-mounted map which gives clearer directions of where the ruins are situated. What's so difficult about designing and printing a new map? The fact that no one has yet done so gives you a clue about shoddy management standards. From the museum’s exit, walk northwest through a small garden to the group of ruins on the shore of the lake known as Parakramabahu Samudera. Then walk east and cross the main road, to the entrance to the other section of the ruins. Your ticket will be checked again. The ruins are in three main clusters: the lakeshore cluster (also known as the ‘island’ group), the royal palace cluster and the quadrangle cluster, each about 500m from each other. But there are plenty more sites scattered a few kilometres around. Some ruins are in bad shape; the ones in the sacred quadrangle are perhaps in the best condition. It wasn’t possible to cover much more than the three main clusters in the time (a daytrip) that I had. Based on my experience, I’d say that if you want to examine most of the ruins, I think you will need a much earlier start, which means staying in Polonnaruwa the night before and the night after. I am rating his site as merely "average". Even allowing for the fact that ruins that are 800 - 1100 years old can't possibly be in good condition, when I compare it with other archaeological sites of similar vintage around the world, Polonnaruwa is not outstanding. The stone construction does not look to have been built to a high standard; the sculpture works were relatively few and not particularly good aesthetically. The fundamental reason, I suppose, is that the kingdom over which Polonnaruwa controlled was probably a smallish one (by world standards) and it might never have had the resources to build a truly great capital city. As a second-class city, today we have second-class ruins. Add to that sub-par management, lack of cafes and toilets in the sites despite the heat and great distances... and my feeling at the end of the day was a degree of dissatisfaction.

We stayed at Sigiri and travelled out each day to Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura. Polonnurawa is certainly worth a visit. There is really a lot of history here. We came with a tour guide so we got the low down on the history. Again expect to pay for the admission which is around 3500 LKR ( pls check before going ) each.  This is about the same price as for Anuradhaphura . The majority of the  entrance fees go towards maintaining the site and further excavations, so you are funding a good cause.  After paying for the admission do go round the museum which is where you get the admission tickets.   The visit to the museum is worthwhile especially if you don’t have a guide. It explains each monument and the history behind it.  And also the history as to why the Kings moved from   Anuradhaphura to Polonnurawa to start a second kingdom. All the places are concentrated in one small area so walking from one to another is quite straightforward. Polonnurawa  started in the 10th Century as the capital city  and ended around the 12th Century . Apparently it had lain undiscovered until British archeologists began probing in the late 19th century when the whole area was covered in forests.  When you look at the buildings do look at the surrounding trees. Their bases are about 1.5 m to 2 m above the ground of the excavations. It will have taken some serious excavations to get to the monuments. Some places are just spectacular.  The Royal palace for one, the second is the lake or a ‘tank’ as they call it.  This huge lake of 25 sq km was manually excavated in the 12th century by people and elephants.  It really is quite an awesome task. There are some temples which are in ruins and previously held the Scared Relic of the Tooth ( now housed in Kandy).  Just do note that the dress code applies to temple ruins as to living temples. No shorts, or crop tops and no slippers on the temple grounds ( even abandoned ones).  A few visitors were caught out and not allowed in. Having visited both Polonnurawa and Anuradhaphura I think if you don’t have enough time then Polonnurawa is the better choice.  But if you have the time and inclination then do visit both places .

Anuradhapura was the capital of ancient Ceylon from about 455BC that was ruled from by successive kings until 1017 when the Cholas from South India captured King Mihindu V, and destroyed much of Anuradhapura and established their own capital at Polonnaruwa. The Cholas lasted until 1070 when the Sinhalese King Vijayabahu drove them out of the island. Vijayabahu retained Polonnaruwa as his capital as did successive kings until the late 13th century. But Polonnaruwa proved difficult to defend against invaders from India and the Sinhalese kingdom moved across to the west coast and Polonnaruwa was allowed to decay. By the late 13th century Ceylon had 2 ancient abandoned capitals although, as ruins, there is still much to see. Anuradhapura is the more extensive and the more important as a religious site for Buddhist pilgrims, whereas Polonnaruwa, the more recent, is in better condition and compact, is considered more important for its archaeology, art, architecture, engineering and agriculture. The ruins of Polonnaruwa are very impressive, demonstrating a remarkable standard of scale, design and construction and, in particular, the detail. There are more than 30 significant buildings and statues here, mostly enclosed within the ancient walls and overlooking the enormous hand dug 2,500 ha Parakrama Samudraya tank as directed by King Parakramabahu I. There are also irrigation tanks and waterways that supplied the gardens and fields. It is believed that King Parakramabahu fully understood the importance of irrigation and is said to have declared that ‘not even a drop of water that comes from the rain must flow into the ocean, without being made useful to man’. On the site is the ticket counter, information centre, small museum, air conditioned auditorium and a small bookshop. But it is the ruined buildings and statues that visitors come to see and a good way to explore those is by hired bicycle. However the vast site is so complex that to best understand it, you would need a guide. Our little party had our own transport and recruited an official guide to show us the sights and provide an informative running commentary. There are both official guides (those with badges) and un-official ones. Our guide was well informed and we felt the cost of R 3,000 was justified. You would need at least 3 hours to cover the entire site including walking around the ruins and taking those essential tourist photographs.

Went here as part of our trip to Sri Lanka and fortunately had an excellent guide with us as this really helped when visiting this site.   The museum was an interesting start followed by a trip around the whole site.  It was truly amazing place and our guide information and explanation brought the place alive.  Clearly one has to dress appropriately and remove one's shoes in places but this shows respect and therefore is clearly not an issue.   A worthwhile place to visit and very well maintained.

The many ruins are spread over a large area so our coach took us from site to site.  The moonstones and guardstones were in an excellent condition.  I stood in quiet contemplation in front of the large stone Buddhas at our last stop.  Very impressive.

I was a bit sceptical to start with visiting Polonnuruwa ruins after previously been to Siem Reap (Angkor Wat) 2 yrs ago. I didnt really know what to expect probably due to my own ignorance but upon visiting with my wife & 2 young kids (8&10), I was very impressed. There are plenty of well retained ruins steeped in history. Its a really interesting bit of history. The ruins are over a large area, you can cycle around or get a guide & transport or if you have a driver use your vehicle. It would be hard to walk around due to the heat. My two daughters struggled a bit with the heat but in their defence they climbed Lion Rock earlier in the morning. I highly recommend visiting the museum to gain a little knowledge before browsing the ruins. Highly recommend visiting this site whilst in the Cultural Triangle.

Best advice is to use a bicycle to visit the area. The place is big but easy with bike and there are plenty for rent around. If you're travelling in a small group my best advice would be to do it ahead of the buses that are all going the same place at the same time. Be smart and observe first where they're going. Then you could be almost alone on the various sites. Half a day is definitely not too much for it and the beauty and peacefuness of the site is really amazing.

We visited this site in early February on a fairly warm day i.e. temperature about 23 degrees. We had guide with us. The advantage of a guide is that they can help you make the most of your visit by selecting out what to see and more importantly they have the knowledge of what is inter-connected and in close proximity too. This is massive heritage site and you cannot explore all of it in one day so selecting out points of interest and finding them is a challenge. Best to read up about it before you arrive as that may help you select out what you think suits you best. Alternatively just meander and explore. There is an option to hire cycles and that could be a good way to explore the site. Whether walking or cycling or with a driver guide you will almost certainly come across structures which will amaze you. The architecture is a delight if you have not previously seen buddhist or hindu heritage sites before. One of the joys was seeing carved granite carvings in the structures which convey stories. Hindu architecture is very different from Buddhist architecture. One revers the Buddha without much reference to the animal kingdom and the other is prolific in carving animals, 'grotesque' masks and moonstones with story telling symbolisms threaded throughout the buildings and statues. One is also relatively simplistic in design while the  other is over complicated, yet they are in harmony too. So this a site where you can marvel at the size and shapes of early structures, whether they be structures like a giant wedding cake or stupa's which are round and dome like. Another joy of visiting this place is the sense of freedom you have to explore it. However there is an obligation that visitors show extra respect for those sites with a special religious significance. This presents no problems if your address is appropriate i.e. no knees (men and women) showing and the female head is covered. However this applies only to certain special places here not all of them. This is also a site that has grass and avenues of trees to contrast with the massive  brick structures. Until I visited this place I never realised that bricks were being made in the 12 century and were being used to build multi storey buildings and places of worship. If you are not keen on heritage ruins and history you will probable not rate these sites very much. For me it was interesting, enjoyable, varied and wonderful because of it heritage. I have not previously seen a nothing quite like it on this scale despite travelling to over 20 countries.

It’s not cheap to get in but you can easily spend hours here. We hired some functional, but quaint, bicycles to get around and needed them. It’s a big site, on a par with Angkor Wat and loads to see. Lots of history, well signed buildings, be aware that many are religious relics and can only be visited in appropriate clothing and barefoot. As it’s so hot, socks helped. Huge number of separate sites, refreshments available around the park and decent toilets at the midpoint. Quiet and a time for reflection, worth checking muse out first.

I always love seeing historical buildings. When it’s about religion and royalty, more is expected. This town shows great culture and history with its huge palace buildings and temple relics. You can see temples with Buddha inside and Hindu on the outside wall. It’s temples, though only relics, you still need to remove shoes and hats before you enter the building. Be careful with the locals who approach you and start to talk about the buildings and history. They will ask for tips once finishes. If you don’t want this service, please don’t let them talk. Cos they will not ask you if you want his service or not but just start it!

Must see in Sri Lanka if you wanna taste the breeze of ancient times. You will feel like in the middle of the jungle, surrounded by monkeys, deer, lizards and flocks of various species of birds. The site is huge and the best way to see it is from a bike. On our way from Dambulla, we just hopped off the bus and there was the guy, lending bikes for 800 Rupies right on the side of the main road. It took us approx. 3 hours to see the whole place and we would have spent there much more time if we were not in hurry.

This is a must do on any trip up into the cultural quarter of Sri Lanka.  This is a UNESO World Heritage site which in its hey day was in the 11th/12th century and was one of the most important cities in Sri Lanka.Overall it is not bad shape! There is so much to see that you should plan on spending 1/2 a day here. You can walk it but it could be quite exhausting and extremely hot and there are no shops for water etc. Hire a bike or better still an A/C car. You should hire a guide as they have a wealth of knowledge  and it will avoid you missing out on stuff. I suggest that you start in the museum (next to where you pay), the head  south to Potugal Hihara, then do the Royal Palace Complex, then the Quadrangle and then work you way up the site to Gal Vihara (the star of the whole show) then head a tad further north to the "Lotus Pond" and finally the Tivanka-Patamaghara ( a hidden gem). Doing the Complex properly makes a great day!

This is a great place to visit in the area and pretty much a must-see. We opted for this rather than anaradhapura as it was nearer, smaller, more compact and better-preserved. You start at the ticket office, which has a museum behind it telling you the history of the site and the temples. It's worthwhile hiring bicycles to get around the temples (they can be got from just outside the site) to speed things up a bit and zip around - inside the site itself the roads are very quiet though you will have a stretch on a fairly busy (and currently under repair) road. You can also get a tuk tuk around it. The royal palace group, quadrangle group and northern group are the main ones you'll visit. There is the "island" group and others further south, but we were hugry and had seen the best-preserved ones by that point and opted not to bother. The ruins are well-preserved and beautifully maintained. You'll have to do a fair bit of taking shoes on and off, and make sure your shoulders and knees are covered as some of the areas are holy and it's a mark of respect. These areas are clearly signposted. All in all it's a great day out.

We where guided trough most of the area and is was so large, but also interesting about the history. It was almost too much in the short time we where here so we got a bit exhausted. But wouldn't liked to missed it. The problem was our tour guide tried to squeeze to hurry up due to the bad wheater it was really poring and he didn't like the rain so much. It would have been nice to take the time we needed but we where on a schedule unfortunatley. Nice area but I recommend you plan to spend at least 3 hours here to be able to take everything in. Museum was not that interesting.

This was a huge area to visit and we were lucky to have a car and chauffeur to move us around and to explain a bit about the ruined temples. Some areas were difficult to walk about on and there was some confusion about where one should take off ones shoes. Sometimes the rough rocky surface deterred shoe removal anyway. A bit of information of the exhibits would have been useful but it left one with an overall impression of past greatness.

This is a truly impressive site with many buildings which have been rebuilt as far as possible.  When found the site was covered in jungle and over many years has been reconstructed.  Certain artefacts are in the museum, where there are scale models of the original buildings.  Visit this either before or after you visit the site to get a true perspective on what the site was like originally.  A guide is recommended to avoid missing the most important buildings and temples.  Socks are recommended on hot days, if you want to visit the temples!

You could easily spend all day here- i'd be hiring a bike next time. We had a whistle stop tour courtesy of our guide Sampath Maragoda- superb guide from our travel company Diethelm Tours. The site is very extensive and worth spending some time exploring

Probably the best historic site of whole Sri Lanka,and ,by far, most popular. It is pretty crowded but it cant spoil the beautiful ruins of this ancient city. We hired a tuk tuk and it took us almost 3 h to go through the whole thing. Highly recommended

This is an important UNESCO world heritage site and has been extensively rebuilt.  It is best visited with a guide.  We spent a couple of hours here, but it would have been easy spend longer.  There are several temples, where shoes have to be removed to enter - a bit of a problem on very hot days, so socks are recommended.  The buildings are quite spaced out so a car is useful.  Tickets are obtainable from the museum further down the main road.

We would highly recommend Polonnarawu (people staying at our guest house who visited both Polonnarawu and Anaradhapura found the latter disappointing in comparison).  Entry is not cheap -  25$ per person – but it is an impressive site, with well-preserved monuments and good landscaping.  It is a generally peaceful site, with a prevailing air of calm and respect.  The one exception was the completely inappropriate loud music blaring from the refreshments area half way round.  We spent around four hours there which enabled us to visit all the temples and monuments.  We spent a further 30 mins in the museum adjoining the ticket office. Practicalities: Polonnarawu covers a large area, so walking the whole site, which covers a large area, might be a challenge - particularly in the 30 degrees heat.  We had hired a driver for the day so he came with us into the site (entry is free for locals) and dropped us off at each of the main areas to wander around at leisure – the car a/c in between stops was very welcome!  Another option is to hire a bike outside the site, which a number of people did ( depending on where you hire bikes from the downside is that you may have to cycle for a stretch on the main road – contending with all the usual crazy Sri Lankan traffic- either at the start of the tour or end).   Socks are recommended when entering the temples as it can be very hot underfoot.  About half way round there are toilets – those for foreigners were clean & in a reasonably good condition.  There were also the aforementioned refreshment stalls.   There are similar facilities (albeit less clean toilets) just before the exit.

This is a World Heritage site and a must if you are in the area.  The place is large, but it is easy to walk the ground to the various sights that are all open to the public.  In some one must remove shoes.  I would suggest that one reads up about this site in advance since there is a lot to absorb.  Also you would be well prepared to ask questions to your guide as you go from one to another.

We visted this archeological site during the morning and the visit took us about 2,5 hours. Our driver was picking us up to transfer us from one place to another and then let the visit quicker. This site, as any other in Sri Lanka, is definitely very expensive if compared with more important and monumental sites in other countries (Angkor Wat, Bagan, Sukothai..). Morover, no comulative ticket is possible. In many cases archeological sites or temples only accept dollars from turists and no credit card. It was our first visit in Sri Lanka, so we decied to enrol a guide we met in front of the museum entry: 1500 rupees. It was interesting to start the visit from the museum, where we could understand some info about the history and see pieces of stones, statues we would recall diring the visit in the outside area. Weather wasn't good despite the dry season.

If there is one place you visit in Central Province this it it. The whole complex covers a vast area, wear good shoes and take plenty of water. The museum is very interesting and each of the various site have jewels in each of them. The highlight for us were the  Weijantha Prasada, Kumara Pukona and Kiri Vehera.

You can go around by car or by bike & (it was raining, so we opted for the former!) as the sights are quite spread out. It’s worth getting a guide here (2,000 LKRs approx at time of writing) as there is quite a bit of ground to cover & as it’s mostly ruins it’s good to have someone to bring it alive for you. An interesting introduction to early Sri Lankan culture & Buddhism.

Awesome place. Get a tuktuk to the top and walk your way back to the exit. You’ll have the place completely to yourself amoungst the ruins and wildlife. It is expensive to get in (20$ each) but if you haven’t already done Anuradhapura ruins 100% do these they’re wonderful!! The walls takes 4/5 hours and is peasey!

We decided to walk to ruins. Grabbed a TuKtuk for 300 to take us all the way to the furthest ruin (the picture house) and then started the walk back. The ruins themselves are really interesting. The site is HUGE! The walk took around 4/5 hours at a very leisurely pace. It’s worth the pennies if you haven’t done the ruins in Anuradhapura.

We spent well over 3 hours here and could have stayed longer, but we had to drive 2 hours to our next destination.  This was a huge city over 1000 years ago and there is a lot here to see.  The best were the three Buddha statues at the end, one seated, one standing, one sleeping, all carved out of the living rock.  Don't miss this place!

I was so disappointed with the ruins. They really are RUINS!. If you have been to Bagan or Angkor Wat you will be bitterly disappointed with this AND it is ridiculously expensive Where you buy the ticket does not even have a map to guide you! It was not obvious beforehand but the whole site is a park which was easy to bike around. Do not make the mistake I made when I re-did the ruins and tried to exit via the entrance boom gate..they made me do 2 kms back to the exit which then involved 2 kms on a very scary main road just to get back to the point where they had refused passage to me!!

We were a party of 3 and unable to bike so walked it and decided that was the best way to go as we saw so much more and did not have to return bikes. Would have taken about an hour to walk the whole thing if we didnt wander around the interesting ruins.  We replenished our bodies with food and water at the couple stalls along the way. We took the 1 hour bus from Habarana to the museum area and picked up our ticket by 9.30am. Would have been better at 8.30am. Morning was full of tourists and by afternoon not many touists at all. Went to the Island area first outside the museum. Then walked out to the public park. Walk left about 200m, across the road and into the second area. The walk under the trees was magnificent. When we came to the pool, it was about noon so we ate iceblcks and rested under the trees until after 1pm. The walked round the sacred area. It too around half an hour to walk to the third section under the trees and we spent the rest of the time exploring here as it was a large area with wells, ancient loos, hospital and other interesting areas. At 5m we popped out at the pond side. We took a tuk tuk for 300 rupee to the bus stop on the road to Habarana. Waited about 15 min then got seats on the next bus. Easy ride home.

Recently visited Sri Lanka and spent a morning (3.5hours) exploring the ancient city at Polonnaruwa. We arrived earlyish ~9:00 and had a driver who took us around the site. It is expensive but well worth a visit!! 1) The museum - lots of site information and an introduction to the history of Buddhism in Sri Lanka with insight into the Hindu influences of some of the buildings. 2) The ancient city - very interesting, beautiful buildings, very different to anything I have seen before in the UK. 3) The 3 Buddhas - lying, standing and sitting - very awe-inspiring. There were people leaving flowers and praying, which was quite moving as it is not just a tourist attraction but a sacred place for many individuals. Tips: - Bring a camera but be respectful, in some places there were signs asking tourists not to take photos with the icons and it was disheartening to see some people ignore this request. Take suncream as the site is mostly exposed with little shade. There are stalls around selling drinks/icecreams etc but we took our own water. Wear easily sandals/slip-on shoes as you have to remove your shoes to see several of the monuments/buildings up close.

Polonnaruwa was my favourite site in the cultural centre of Sri Lanka. It was extremely hot so it’s best to make an early start to see as much as you can before it gets too hot. The whole area is very beautiful with many ruined buildings, sculptures, tombs, huge Buddhas and stupas. The area is huge so we went in an air conditioned car with a guide but many younger people were on bikes and using a guide book. I particularly enjoyed the huge stupas and the moss covered tombs which were set under shady trees. Beautiful and great for photography! I recommend that you do some research before you go to decide which parts of Polonnaruwa interest you most.

Wonderful complex of ruins. World class sites in a glorious green park. We much preferred our day at Polonnaruwa, mainly for the greater sense of atmosphere and solitude, and wealth of detailed beautiful sites. In my view a bike is unnecessary, as long as you are comfortable walking (all flat terrain. We saw almost everything and walked ~15k. One suggestion - if you are looking for a peaceful visit try and arrive as early as you can (park opens at 7.30) and then visit the quadrangle first, before heading all the way to Gal Vihara and then working your way back to the entrance. For us, this minimised crowds nicely. Head through the museum last to spend some brief time looking at the miniature models of the key sites.

The best way to visit the ruins is certainly by bicycle. Time visit of the site: approx. 3h. Entrance fee: 3750LKR ($25) for 1 day only. You buy the ticket at the museum (beside the canal). It is very expensive if you compare with the entrance fee of other ancient sites, in S-E Asia for instance (all many times cheaper than this one). During our bicycle tour, we have been controlled 4 times, which was a bit annoying, also because only "westerners" without guides were controlled. Some sites are well preserved, but some are not interesting, such as the Royal Palace, very disappointing, nothing to see, just 2 walls which could have been anything else... that was my least favorite site of the ruins. Beware the monkeys, they can be mean. Twice, we saw monkeys attaking people. We also saw lot of interesting birds and monitor lezards, which made the visit more agreable. Beware the touts trying to sell you small elephants in wood. They will ask you for 3000 LKR (around $20) but in the end, they are ready to sell them for 300LKR ($2), so 10 times cheaper. Don't get ripped off.

If you do this and it is well worth a couple of hours then a bike is essential. You simply cannot walk this!! Avoid our frustration, the visitor centre is on the other side of the main road from the ruins. If you come out and turn left down the main road you can enter the ruins after about 400m on the right. Take the first opportunity to hire a bike, it's only about £3 and it doesn't matter really on the quality. I hired one opposite the entrance and it's the worst bike in Asia but added to the fun. Most of the important sights are off the main drag, just leave your bike and take off your shoes. We wore trousers. The locals like you to do this out of respect but there is no need if you don't wish to. Many people wear shorts. Cost was $25 each.

This is a wonderful site to visit.  Not as wide spread as Anurandhapura, but still large enough to warrant a full day there if you have the energy and enthusiasm.  We were taken round by our guide in a car, but a lot of people rent bicycles, which are really the ideal way of getting around this huge complex .Polonnaruwa was the second Ancient Capital of SL, only being built around 1000AD. After it was abandoned some 150 years later, the jungle took over and it was only in the last century, after the British left around 1957 that archaeologists started their work in bringing it to the wonderful site it is now.  There are so many places to see and visit and you really need a guide to show you the best way round and provide the stories to the many wonderful buidings you see.  Near the entrance is a very interesting and informative museum, which is well worth a visit, before you journey round the site, with many reconstructions of what you will see.. Make sure you give yourself plenty of time to visit Gal Vihara, which is towards the rear of the site. This where 4 giant Buddhas have been carved out of a single huge rock and are breathtaking; the reclining Buddha alone is worth the visit.  Just to point out that although ruins, many of the temples are still holy places and require you to cover up accordingly and remove your shoes.  Best to wear footwear that slips off easily and take a pair of socks, to cover your feet as the ground which is very rocky can get quite hot

The area has an incredible history and some of the sites are absolutely stunning. However, the 35 USD entrance fee makes for an expensive outing. We biked through which was slightly spoiled by the number of trucks and cars on the same road. Note that you will need to remove your shoes to access the temples so flip flops are ideal or on a hot day wear thick socks to not burn your feet on the concrete. Also know that you will need to cover your knees and shoulders and avoid taking photos with your back to any Buddha statues

Along with the elephant gathering the main reason to visit this area. I rented a bicycle which is probably the best way to experience it. It can be pretty busy. Anuradhapura is scattered old city, and we were told that so is Polonnaruwa with a lot to explore within smaller distance. So we chose the latter. Beautiful ruins - could take you almost a day to explore them at leisure. The museum is among the best in Sri Lanka. That's where you can buy the tickets. Expensive, but worth it! And the tickets are not sold at all the gates. Best to explore on a rented bicycle. The quadrangle, Vatadage and Gal Vihara were simply outstanding!

Well worth a visit if nearby. Flat walking in a large, spread- out complex, like a park setting. Worth visiting the museum first to get the history and see the model reconstructions of the buildings. We had our guide, which enhanced our visit. Allow a half day, and time for refreshments afterwards.

The scale of the complex - one the capital of the country- is staggering. We spent a half day there, with a guide, the expense of which is most worthwhile. We started with a tour of the museum, which helps in the understanding of both the scale and purpose of the site. A “must see” on any trip to Sri Lanka.

I would suggest choosing either Polonnaruwa OR Anuradhapura as they are very similar and then go to Mihintale. The ruins at Polonnaruwa are very impressive and it's a lovely way to spend a day wandering around them. We had a driver so he was taking us from car park to car park to save time...however renting a bicycle would be a great idea and it's safe to cycle around.

This is a major archaeological site.  It's going to consume the better part of a day, but it is well worth it.  Be advised that it is expensive by Sri Lankan standards. Only the southern complex seems to be free of charge.  The other locations require a ticket good for a day.  A couple will cost you slightly over 70,000 rupees. The town is ugly and dusty, amplified by ongoing roadworks, and the high level of harassment due to the touristy nature of the ruins extends to the town.  Everything costs more than other towns - there are occasional good restaurants but they also cost more (Rama on the main road has a good veg buffet for 350).  I stayed in the north of the town by the lake, which was very pleasant and convenient enough if your touring the ruins by tuktuk or bicycle (cycling the busy main road is a hassle but there's a shoulder for most of it and the roadworks has slowed down traffic - there are also interesting back roads that you could try).  Still, the ruins and dagobas are spectacular, even if entry is expensive and the vendors and beggars are horrible.  Allow 5 hours to see them on a bicycle.

There's much more harassment here than at Anuradhapura or Sigiriya, including begging children, forceful vendors and snake charmers who shout at anyone who takes a photo within 50 metres of them without paying.  The range of ruins and dagobas is almost but not quite as good as Anuradhapura.  The main sites are full of bus tours but there are a lot of opportunities to get off the road and see some interesting complexes.  Tuktuk drivers charge 2000 or less for a tour but I really enjoyed seeing them by bicycle - it's easy to cycle from the museum and the connected palace complex down the lakeside Bund to the southern group, then when you enter the main group just north of the museum, the rest is all one big complex that's nice and flat and easy to cycle around (then you have to exit in the north of the complex), only cycling on the main road is a hassle.  Took me about 5 hours to see everything on a bicycle.

My fiancé and I came to Polonnaruwa with not many expectations. It was one of those sights you had to see when you came to Sri Lanka, but it definitely did not disappoint. It actually blew us away! Once we got there we hired an English speaking tour guide who was wonderful. He suggested we started with the museum to give us context on what we were going to see, which we highly recommend. It is incredible what people could build over 2,000 years ago, but even more incredible that you can see many remaining structures of their detailed craftsmanship today. I have been to Athens before and imagine seeing the 30 foot statue of Aphrodite in the temple built for her… that’s what you get in some of the ruins at Polonnaruwa. Many of the Buddha statues are still in tact and you can really imagine life in this empire thousands of years ago.

The ruins that you can see are vast, but they are only a small fraction of the total site, most of which is still covered by earth and trees. There are some fantastic examples unearthed and the scale is breathtaking. Unfortunately war has taken its toll and key buildings were torched albeit centuries ago. It is well worth a visit and needs a few hours because of the sheer size of the site. The on-site museum has some interesting artifacts and good evidence of surgical tools from a thousand years ago.

Worth a visit. The palaces and temples are really nice and interesting. Sometimes there are just some ruins left, but sometimes you can still find a well maintained temple and statutes. The tickets for the archeological site have to be bought at the museum and include the museum as well. The museum is really recommended, as you get a good overview of the history of Sri Lanka and thanks to the models you get an idea how the temples and palaces have looked liked, as some of them are nowadays only ruins. The whole site is very big so a bicycle, tuktuk or driver (cars are also allowed on the whole site) is really recommended. We have been there with our driver, which was really nice, as he knew where to go to get to the next place and could also tell us some of the history behind the temples/ruins. As there are also temples inside the archeological site, knees and shoulders should be covered, it is also recommendable to wear or at least bring socks as you have to take off your shoes before entering a holy site and the stones can be really hot. The price however is too expensive (25$/person) for what it is (compared to Angkor Wat which costs 15$/person and the whole temple site is much bigger). But the prices for all the temples in Sri Lanka are very expensive, if you are not a local, for whose it is for free.
