Incredible ruins of an ancient city. We visited late afternoon to avoid the heat of the day - and finished our tour in a thunder storm! Loved it! You will need a few hours to get around everything, but it is worth the time. You can rent a bicycle to get around which would be great to do.

I visited the ancient city ruins this morning. Travelled by bus from Negombo to Kurunegala and then on another bus to Polonnaruwa, the entire journey took a little over 5 hours. The current entrance fee is USD 25 and they accept both dollars and rupees. The ticket gives you access to a museum located where the ticket office is as well as the ruins (these are some 5 min by bicycle). A long story short, the place is mildly amusing and surely something to tick off on your todo list while in Sri Lanka but if you are thinking "ancient city" along the lines of Angkor or Bagan you're in for a nasty surprise as this is ways less in terms of things to see. I'd say that if Angkor is 5 stars in the impressive category the ruins we are talking about is 2 or 1. There are 2 large stupas, one white and another black, lots of small walls and half ruined small columns, a few statues still in good condition, plus a modest temple and that's pretty much it. And the monkeys, big crowds and rather entertaining. Things to keep in mind: - makes sense to hire a bicycle (LKR 500) but walking seems an ok option too if you have plenty of time - don't lose your ticket - they checked mine 4 times - there are many souvenir sellers strategically located to cover every ruin - ticket price doesn't feel adequate for what you get (say $10 would be ok) - buses are often too packed around 5-6 pm and don't even stop for you, which means that they don't feel you can be squeezed in at all not to mention seated - once you're in, bottled water asking price is around LKR 100 per 1.5L which is comparable to the price at the convenience stores

We hired a driver to take us from habarana, around the site and back to the hotel for 5000 rupees. He took us to the museum first to purchase our tickets (3850 rupees per adult). The site is controlled by guards and you will be stopped and asked to show your tickets often. The staff at the ticket office are very friendly, it was a nice change from the previous day in Anuradhapura where the lady who sold us our tickets lied and said she didn't have any change (which she was able to produce when we suggested we underpay given we didn't have any 100 rupee notes). Our driver took us to the main 6 sites which took approximately three hours, including the museum. We went a bit later in the day (arrived around 11am) and so it was very hot by the time we were finishing around 2am. I can recommend going early in the day when it is cooler. Some (but not all) sites require shoe removal and modest dress. It pays to take something you can use to cover knees and shoulders if your clothing is not adequate. This is a wonderful site, recommended to all tourists.

The historic site is in an enclosed area with the key attractions located relatively close by. It is conserved pretty well and there are a lot of attractions to see. I would recommend this as the best place in Sri Lanka to see many attractions fast as they are located close by and in good condition. However, due to the heat, it will be challenging to walk from one venue to the other. Best would be to rent a bike or have a driver. Bottle of water, a cap and sunglasses would be helpful. Also when entering some religious places you will need to remove shoes. Avoid long holidays as it will be crowded.

Polonnaruwa is best explored by Bicycles. the well planned ancient medieval capital thrived in civilization in the 11th and 12th century. the monuments are fascinating, both in Buddhist and Dravidian structures which conveys its past. it is a Unesco world heritage site

Too many obnoxious tourists on the site. All we saw were ruins of old buildings, more statues more Buddhist temples and nothing unique that you can't find anywhere else in Sri Lanka. It consists of a lot of temples and religious buildings. The good thing is that all the religious sites are close to each other, it was soooo hot that we got the driver to drive to the different locations hop off explore and on to the next.

There were extensive and interesting ruins in Polonnaruwa scattered over a fair distance.  From our experience, it is best to visit all of these with a driver, as we did, who will drop you off, tell you what to see and pick you up when you are finished.  4 or 5 hours is enough.  It is not necessary to stay the night as this visit can easily be done in a day trip from Sigirya. I agree with the comment that your feet get burned a lot.  Wear short socks.  I also agree that there could have been have been more info about each site.   I also agree that we “enjoyed this better than Anuradhapura”, which for us was underwhelming, and rated third in the cultural triangle sites for us.   We did not object to the 25 USD as it must cost a lot to preserve all these fabulous historical and cultural sites.  I objected more to the cost of the driver to take us there and back.

This ancient city is a great thing to visit in Sri Lanka.  Firstly visit the museum and get tickets - the museum has a lot of information but no photography is allowed sadly.  Then go and hire some bikes.  The main entrance is just down the road and on the opposite side to the museum - some arbitrary guys hanging around there will rent you a bike for a negiotable rate (very cheap, just a few GBP).  There are 3 ticketed places to visit within the large archaelogical site, but that is only a fraction of the total number of monuments you can see.  We really liked the idea of a bike, as the distances are very large (huge site) and walking one end to another would take many hours.  The bike introduces a fun aspect to the trip and allows you to easily customise which ruins you see and when.  If for some reason you can't get a bike, tuk tuks are available to take you around.  A side note: there are signs warning you, but don't take photos where your back is facing the buddhas (or selfies) - that's not considered respectful and the guards will not be happy.  A very fun, full day event.

Polonnaruwa area shows the evidence that Sri Lankan are grate architectures. polonnaruwa are contain lot of man build tanks, temples,  Castles, monuments, Ponds etc. Better to travel in a vehicle and observe the area. avoid rainy seasons, dry seasons may be too hot

Like many others, we were recommended to rent a bicycle which we did. But then had to bike about 100 m down the road to go buy tickets for the entrance to the ruins (which was right across from the rental place!). Doesn't seem far, but with construction and two narrow lanes of classic Sri Lanka traffic (tuk tuks, mopeds, trucks, buses, cars etc.), it was a fairly harrowing experience! Expensive to get in, maybe 3800 rps per person, no map provided so we took photo of the one on the wall of the museum. IT was also 35 degrees and the cycle paths don't have a lot of shade, so prepare to stop frequently and rest! And bring a hat! Also, we skipped one (the famous Buddha ruin) which you require one ticket for (inclusive in the entrance price) and the gate keepers were so confused as to why we were leaving without seeing this. It's because we were extremely tired and dehydrated! Asked for our passports (which we didn't have) and milled around for 10 minutes wondering why we want to leave. I never knew leaving a place could be so challenging. They ended up stamping our tickets "cancelled" and saying "you can not return". IT was a frustrating end to what would have been a really beautiful day. That said, highly recommend seeing all the ruins just be prepared for the heat and $$$ overheads!

Wow! It was so fascinating to be taken back to the 12th century, and see the ruins built by the 3 original Buddhist kings. We had a fantastic guide from the museum who then took us to the sites. We saw some visitors doing bike tours, which looked fun, but hot.

I rented a bike in the town and rode for a few hours through the ruins. The ruins are well preserved and interesting. We visited this place on our 16 day tour through Sri Lanka. Although we have visited Yapahuwa as well I must admit that this place is far more impressive. The area is very wide spread and offers different temples, ponds, houses and Buddha statues from this period. Of course it strongly reminds on the locations of the Indiana Jones movies ;-) Please consider that even with a guide you will need at least 3 hours to visit to most important and impressive locations there.

Polonnaruwa is quite spectacular, even if you're not hardcore into ruins and archaeology!  We debated paying the US$ 25 entree fee, but really glad we did.  It's well worth it!  The highlight is the Gal-Vihara stone carved Buddhas, but there are also many other sights worth stopping at.  You buy your entry ticket at the museum and then can drive or rent a bike to cover the extensive grounds of the ruins.  Don't try to walk unless you are very eager for exercise as the distances are substantial.  You'll need about 3 hours to enjoy the main highlights of the complex (slightly less if you hurry; more if you're into careful scrutiny). Suggestions: - visit the museum first, upon buying your ticket, but don't spend too much time there; the displays are only average, but they do give you some insights into the highlights in the archaeological park - go early, if possible (it gets hot and crowded, especially on weekends) - wear a hat or sunscreen (or both) - take plenty of water (although you can also readily buy water in the park) - prepare to remove your shoes to visit the sacred spots - show respect (especially in photographing the Buddha images)

Many reviewers have complained about the US$25 entrance fee, but don't be deterred by these reviews.  The complex of ruins and ancient structures are well worth the entrance fee.  People spend $1500 or $2000 or more to travel to Sri Lanka and then complain about $25 fee to see world-class archeological treasures... come on! Start your tour at the museum, but don't spend too much time there.  The real highlight of the place are the ruins and ancient structures. Work your way through the numerous structures in the complex, concluding with the highlight at Gal Vahera, which is exceptional.  The entire complex is huge and the best way to see the place is to rent a bike or ride with your driver if you have the luxury.

I recommend going really early as it was scorching hot by midday and you have to walk around some of the sites barefoot which was like walking on hot coals!  Other than that it was really interesting and lots of grey langurs and torgue macaques around the ruins

I really liked this historical centre.  We visited mid-week on rather a dull day and therefore it was very quiet, with easy access to the various ruins.  Within the inner citadel there are the very impressive remains of the royal palace, but the whole area is littered with well-preserved ruins that still give a good idea of what they must have been like in their heyday over 1000 years ago. Polonnaruwa is spread over a large area and is perhaps a bit much to be covered on foot.  We had our own car, but more energetic visitors hired bikes.  This is another site where hiring an official guide is probably a good investment.  The Polonnaruwa Museum is an excellent place to visit at the end of the tour as it has some good model reconstructions of the main buildings which put the whole site into some sort of perspective. The various ruins here at Polonnaruwa seemed slightly more varied than at Anuradhapura and a visit is highly recommended for those interested in history and architecture.

The ruins of Polonnaruwa are a must visit site of Sri Lanka. Although the city was of lesser importance to Anuradhapura, the ruins are much better preserved and are far more compact. The entrance ticket for foreigners is exorbitantly high, at 25$ per person, whereas the locals pay next to nothing.

Despite the high cost of entry this was one bit of Sri Lanka that we really enjoyed. Being able to drive from area to area was a great asset and there was sufficient remains of the old buildings to get a feel for just how the royals lived all those years ago surrounded by thousands of monks and many temples. The signposting is also good with just enough information and so it is easy to understand what you are seeing. For those interested in the past history of Sri Lanka I would definitely recommend this visit.

One piece of advice is to get in early (opens 730am) and ride all the way to the back where there is no one around. We did this and had the place to ourselves for over 2 hours which made for much better photos and a much more historical experience. By mid morning thousands of people will be all over the complex.

My husband and I toured the ruins by bicycle -- a great way to see so many interesting ruins at your own pace.  The museum is good also.  None of the national parks or major attractions in Sri Lanka are cheap, so you need to take that into consideration, but we thought it was well worth it.

Our driver found him in the car park before we went into the ruins. His english was very good. You are supposed to have cover shoulders and knees, and ideally wear white or light colours(out of respect) but a lot of tourists didn't, and it was ok. We were told that you should not take photos with your back to any of the buddahs as it is disrespectful.

Consider at least 3 hours to visit.

We visited Polonnaruwa on a day trip from Habarana, about an hour by bus. We got dropped off in the old town, a few hundred meters from the ticket office. We were immediately approached by people renting out bikes, so that was easily settled. 300 rupee for the day, and you can even get a bike for 200 if you walk a bit further. Ticket price might seem steep at 25 dollar, but as long as it goes to the maintenance of the site I'm ok with that. And the park does look well maintained, well paved roads, good information, clean site. Biking around the site is nice and easy, the major sights cover a distance of about 5 km. Good to remember is that most of the buildings and ruins are still considered holy places, so appropriate dress is required  (though nobody seemed to make an issue of shorts just above the knee for men). Wear easy shoes, you'll be going in and out of them the whole time. Wear socks or something because the ground gets hot and walking barefoot can be quite uncomfortable. The sights themselves are of varying interest in my opinion, a lot is not more than some brick walls and pillars. Many places have interesting details though, and the big dagobas are impressive. In the citadel, the audience hall was much more interesting than the royal palace. The Quadrangle holds the most major sights, and the statues at Gal Vihara are beautiful. The museum at the entrance is included in the price and worth a quick visit. It has a lot of info on the site and some nice and interesting models of how the buildings might have looked back in the day. Also some very pretty bronze statues that were found on site. We skipped the southern group, after more than 3 hours we had enough old stuff for one day :-). After a quick lunch near the bus stop, we were back on our way home.

Polonnaruwa is the main town of Polonnaruwa District in the North Central Province, Sri Lanka. Kaduruwela area is the Polonnaruwa New Town and the other part of Polonnaruwa, remains as the royal ancient city of polonnaru kingdom. Polonnaruwa ruins The second most ancient of Sri Lanka's kingdoms, Polonnaruwa was first declared the capital city by King Vijayabahu I, who defeated Chola invaders in 1070 to reunite the country once more under a local leader. The Ancient City of Polonnaruwa has been declared a World Heritage Site.

This is an amazing complex with so much history and architecture. If you love ruins then this is for you. We hired a guide which really helped explain some of the amazing things here and the history. We were a bit pushed for time but allow half a day if you like taking photos. If you can get there at opening you will skip some of the large tour groups. Highly worthwhile.

Spectacular though these ruins are for $25 (Cash only) a head they could at least provide a map in English (or French or Spanish) and be courteous when they take your money. If you prefer, as I do, not to take a guide I suggest you have your own guidebook to hand to try and make some sense of it. There are few signs or information boards outside the museum.

Polonaruwa We traveled from Trincomalee to Polonaruwa to see the ruins of the second capital city of Sri Lanka following the demise of Anuradhapura. These ruins had like so many cities in this area had been depopulated by the malaria mosquito and for 700 years were abandoned to the jungle. They were rediscovered in the 1890's since when reconstruction and archeological digs have continued. Here is the remains of a seven story palace who's construction can be seen in the Archeological Museum. Along side the palace was the audience room with eighteen columns and a throne for the king. Sixteen councillors would attend the Kings Councils each standing to attention next to one of the columns. There is a circular temple with stairs leading to the inner sanctuary past one of four Buddha each facing a cardinal point. Next to this is the only Cambodian style square Stupa in Sri Lanka. Nearby are some of the only rock carvings of Buddha remaining in the world. A truly amazing experience.

Polonnaruwa covers a very large area so be prepared to walk a lot.  Either have a car, tuk tuk or bicycle to get between sites as they are quite spread out. While (vijayabahu's )victory and shifting of kingdoms to the more strategic Polonnaruwa is considered significant, the real Hero of Polonnaruwa  of the history  It was his reign that is considered the Golden Age of Polonnaruwa. Trade and agriculture flourished under the patronage of the king who was so adamant that no drop of water falling from the heavens was to be wasted and each was to be used toward the development of the land. Hence, irrigation systems that are far superior to those of the Anuradhapura Age were constructed during Parakramabahu's reign - systems which to this day supply the water necessary for paddy cultivation during the scorching dry season in the east of the country. We two females feel we were very lucky that no more happened in this incident. We felt very safe in all other areas of the sites. Please be careful when going down this road.

Came here by bus from Dambulla (100lkr each way). Hired a tuk tuk to take us round based on reviews. Glad we did. Was so hot. Cycling would've done me in. I drank 1 1/2 litres of water in 2 hrs it was that hot. Tuktuk was more than I wanted to pay (2000lkr) but couldn't argue down. Entrance ticket cost 3550lkr each. They got shirty with people who tried to pay with 5000 notes and not correct change. Keep your ticket handy. You need to show it at least twice. Including when leaving the compound. Take/wear socks. You have to take your shoes off a lot. Don't think it's cool to have bravado and go without. It's hot and it hurts. Even when wearing socks I had to pace around to stop the burn. I'm quite a 'shoes off' person, so I'm not talking from a baby soft footed, pedicured perspective. Wear the socks!! Take water. You can also buy it there at a mark up (150lkr for 500ml). Take something to cover your shoulders. Scarves/sarongs are fine. Trousers/ankle length skirts not essential. I wore knee length shorts and this caused no problem. We didn't have a guide so just took our own time, talked about each place. Read the given info. If you have imagination and general historical understanding that is sufficient.

After picking several locations to visit in Sri Lanka this was indeed one of the biggest for me. It did not disappoint great tour provided by www.manutoursrilanka.com  from Cinnamon Bey Beruwale resort Manu can be found on the beach  nice guy not pushy and eager to please and the money goes into the local economy. This trip formed part of our main excursion to covering Kandy Polonnaruwa. This ancient city that had been  the royal capital of Chola and Sinhalese abandoned and laid undiscovered in the rain forest, for hundreds of years to be discovered by British in the 19th century.  The site is  still being cleared today. In 1982 was added to UNESCO world heritage list. We picked up our guide who joined our party, as we drove around the site  he explaining the history of the  city and its remains stopping along the way alighting for photos an explanation of the buildings the highlight for me was the standing and sleeping Buda, 📸 jaw dropping  feat of ancient craftsmanship painstakingly carved into the rock face. Hiring bikes is also a good option.  We left here and headed back to our hotel prior to going to Minneriya  national park for a dusk safari.

Initially we were going to hire bikes for the day but decided on the car and AC... good decision as the temp reached 32 deg.  If wanting to do this amazing tour bu bike then could I suggest early morning or late afternoon.  The site is very big, don't know how many sq km and a guide is essential to explain everything.  You could spend all day here.  Some lovely buildings, stupas and Buddhas and shows how advanced society was all those years ago... Well worth a visit and use a guide....

If you like archaeological sites, this is one of the ruins you must visit with history of over 2,000 years.   Well maintained and lots to see.   You will be asked to take your shoes off at some places so be prepared to have a "BBQ"sole on a hot day!  Bring thick socks :) The whole site is open so bring a brolly or a hat.  So much to see in one day.

We went here while staying in Dambulla (1 1/2 hours away). We took a Taxi there as it was a Van he had with Air Con. They all want to rip you off where they can but don't let them! Convert rupees into our money when you're there everywhere you go so you can know exactly how much things costs and get them down in price. The taxi was the best option for us as you will find this place is HUGE! You can't possibly walk around it all because it's so hot and big (plus in different parts) The taxi took us to all the main temples/ruins to see from using my book I took with me from home and he was brilliant. He stopped and let us out to view each one and then drove on to the next one. It's boiling hot so take water and wear a hat and sun tan lotion. It took us about 2 hours maybe in total to see them all (you could take longer but we found after Thailand amazing temples/ruins you can't beat them) this was good but not like them. Cost = 3550 rupees each (£18.80) each. Quite dear but OK as there are lots to see. People were riding their bicycles around too so you could do that if you really wanted but it is a LONG way around and in different places so I wouldn't have coped doing that.

This is a must see on any visit to Sri Lanka. The site is huge and to explore it all well you need a whole day. If you don't have that amount of time the king's palace, swimming pool and several of the larger temples easily gives you a taste of what it was like. The temples do expect you to cover shoulders and  knees ( the latter for females only) and will hand out shawls/scarves if you are inappropriately dressed. A word of warning, everyone must take their shoes off to visit the temple. The ground is red hot and will burn your feet so take some thick socks to wear. You may not look cool but it will save you a great deal of pain!

This is a wonderful UNESCO  site. It reminded me of Pompei. However it is spread over a large area-so bikes are useful,or your driver can ferry you around the complex. Some of the statues are in poor condition. The museum is informative-so spend an hour getting to know the history. Also, be prepared to remove shoes, slippers etc. before entering the temples-the floor can get very hot on a sunny day. During a visit to one of the temples we noticed newborn puppies and mother sheltering from the sun. Surprisingly none of the priests could be bothered to offer water to the family. They couldn't care less. All the foreign visitors showed concern, and we managed to buy some milk from a street vendor to offer to mum. Not a lot of 'love' evident from so-called 'holy men'

Polonnaruwa was a great city in Sri Lanka which came in to prominence during its' brief period of 2 Centuries of Sri Lankan history.Kings ruled the central plains of Sri Lanka from Polonnaruwa 800 years ago, when it was a thriving commercial and religious centre. Polonnaruwa historical significance sustain area. By studying the ancient city of Polonnaruwa clear about the matter. The country's capital, Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa era was.Parakramabahu the kingdom sometime I city. Polonnaruwa large lakes and pagodas become the proof that there was a human settlement which appear developed in this city.

We really visited this site at the wrong time of the day I would recommend early morning or late afternoon. Its sunny; dry and unforgiving but like most things in the cultural triangle of immense cultural significance of a highly developed ancient civilisation. Like anuruadphura it is vast and you simply cannot take all of it in in a single afternoons sightseeing! The buddhas and the image houses are different but no less interesting to what you will see further north.

Loads of ruins to see at this site, spread over a huge area. You will need a vehicle of some sort to get round as it is impossible to do the whole thing on foot.  You don't necessarily need a guide but some guidance from a book would be useful and make it more interesting. Entrance is US25 payable in LKR in cash only.  Children 6-12 are half price. Take loads and loads of water and best to wear like no trousers and have shoulders covered as you will be going in and out of shrines.

Stunning ruins, some well preserved. The scale is extraordinary. Go early because the heat is oppressive. Some ruins are still considered sacred, so women are expected to cover their legs and shoulders.  Bikes highly recommended because of the size of the complex - once inside there is very little traffic.

We visited the place after reading the history at the museum. We rented two bikes for 700 LKR and thankfully we did rent them. The different sites are not so far apart but there are many of them and using a bike will save you a lot of time. Do bring something to cover your shoulder and you will have to remove your shoes to visit the ruins.  I advise you to bring socks since the floor will be very hot. These ruins have no more ceiling of roofs. Fascinating to see such big civilization left in dust.

Reviewing this on the basis of being home now and comparing it to loads of other things we saw,  Anuradhapura, Dambulla, Mihintale, Sigiriya etc...and in my opinion it is ok but preferred some of the other spots. Lets run through logistics, it is if memory services me right spread over 3 or 4 'areas', with long, long walks in between, our guide waited for us and drove us, it was brutally hot and I am not sure we could have walked. Lots were cycling, even that looked hard work. The 1st 3 x areas are ruins with a few temples, told we needed sarongs but no one was wearing them, did take shoes off. There was a stupa and it was all fine but it was hot (have I mentioned it was hot before?) We got to the Gal Vihara part and lo and behold monkeys everywhere. We skipped Buddha(apologies but baby monkeys are cute) and sat and watched the monkeys for an hour. We don't come across as a very cultured family do we? Anyway, its a must do (yawn) but we watched monkeys scratch their bits and play so not all was lost on us. By the way it was very hot and our guide told us it is always very hot there, not humid just baking at 240c oven hot.

It is an archaeological complex however for me it turned out to be a tick in the box as apart from Gal Vihare I didn't find anything else interesting. I went in May and it was boiling hot. We hired bikes but my friends and I were harassed to buy souvenirs. At the end we were so tired, we didn't even go to all sites. We did take some nice pictures. Unless you are very interested in history and archeology or you just want to go for the sake of going, this is not for you. Plus there is nothing to do in the town.

I would definitely recommend visiting Polonnaruwa despite the hefty entrance fee of $25. I could go on about the 'foreign tourist' entrance fee rant but I'll stop there! We had a guide for our visit and he was fantastic. We got just enough information to make it interesting and I found it very enjoyable. The site is impressive, it reminded me of the Angkor temples. For lovers of ancient history, this is a must. While Europe was in the dark ages, here was a city with advanced culture, science and government. You must get a guide , otherwise you won't appreciate what you are seeing. Take your time so you don't succumb to the heat and make sure you go in a car or van. It is too big to walk around.

If you want to experience a bit of culture then Polonnaruwa is the place to head to. There is plenty to see and can take up an afternoon easily. The only downside I would say is that it can get very busy with large groups which can spoil the atmosphere.

Interesting to learn about the history of Sri Lanka & Buddhism. Museum a good place to start to put the rest of the trip in context. Wish we'd hired bikes & cycled. Found the locations very relaxing & good imagine why a King would locate his palace there. Glad we brought flip-flops for quick entry into the Temples

Unlike Anaradapura the sites here are very easy to access being inside one long 'park' and well worth a visit. We took our 6 year old so we didn't cycle but that's how I would do it. We had our driver drop us at strategic points. It was VERY hot so bring plenty of water.

You will see a lot of stones and more stones and all have a different age and a different size and also you can see what it was when it was earlier because the signs are telling you. If you're interested in such things this will be the place for you otherwise I wouldn't reccommend

The ruins of Polonnaruwa are well maintained. The museum is excellent. Two cautions. Wear socks. We were there on a hot, sunny day. You must remove shoes and hats to enter many of the sacred areas. The sand and stones burned our feet! Guard  your tickets. The three little tabs may fall off. You need specific tabs to enter the museum, Royal Palace Group and Gal Vihara. My wife was denied access to Gal Vihara to see the four Buddhas because we lost that tab.

There is no stunning view or breath-taking monumemt here - it requires more of an appreciation with time spent going from one location to another, perhaps best done by bicycle as we saw many tourists do so. The ensemble is worth the recommended two to three hours, so as to appreciate the variety and diversity of preserved areas. On that note, while I usually don't stop at the museum, it was useful to get a sense of the vastness of the religious site and what it used to look like - a useful start right by the ticketing counter.

Worth spending half a day touring all the sites. Rent a car as the weather can get  bearably hot and humid. It's a good way to learn the Sri Lanka culture and how tolerant ancient folks were tolerant of other religions. Bring back the good times!

Rent a bike, that is so much fun when exploring this ancient city! First start at the museum for your dayticket (25 dollars. Ons price, museum and complex) and to get a first view on the history plus some of the artifacts they found in Polonnaruwa. After that go to the complex and visit all the sights. It will take approx. 6~7 hours to see everything by bike. Do not forget to wear a t-shirt that covers your shoulders and a pants that covers your knees!!!

This is a 'must see' on the Sri Lanka itinerary if you like old ruins. The rock-hewn Buddhas, temples and other ruins are fascinating and easily navigable by bicycle (start early because it gets hot). Even my children seemed to sort of enjoy the half-day visit. Good value for the $25 entry fee.

would definitely recommend hiring a bike for this. We went there ealry in the morning so it's not too hot just yet and you can easily bike around without seeing any tourist. Great :) Don't forget to bringt enough water and a hat ;)

We visited Polonnaruwa by bike - as do most of the visitors. But we found a bike with a babyseat for our 4 year old and a childrensbike for our 5 year old! Best day ever, cycling was fun and Pollonnaruwa is gorgeous and very uncomplicated to visit.

We did this as part of our 4 day tour with PL Tours. Our very knowledgeable driver Sarath said the time to go is a bit later to avoid the crowds and it's a bit cooler. We arrived at Polonnaruwa about 3.30/4 - he dropped us at the museum we we walked round (there was one other couple in there) then he drove us to the site. We walked round the first bit using our guide book, popped back in the van and drove onto the second bit and so on. We saw all 5 types of monkeys and were not bothered by any of them. The crowds had gone and some of the parts like the temple we had to ourselves. The Buddha's carved into the Rock were beautiful. Definitely worth a visit but can be knocked off in 2 or 3 hours if you just want a pleasant wander rather than an in depth guided tour.

We used a guide and biked the area (would recomend both!). See a lot of sights - museum and all the ruins which are beautiful. Guide gave valuable info on the history and the buildings former uses. Bike was a good way of getting around as quite a large area (easy cycling as flat). Don't forget to cover legs and shoulders as without you won't be able to enter some areas!

Travelled out to see the ruins which were interesting but it is a lot of walking in the heat and it is very similar all over the location and lots of temples. Would not recommend going out of your way to visit but ok if you're in the area.

Do a bike visit around the different places...to see all main things it takes 2-3 hrs i think. It will be hot so go early...and make sure as women to cover legs in all temple areas. Tickets are 25 usd pp. We enjoyed especially the temples where budda teeth were kept by the kings...one of the main sites

I've been visiting Polonnaruwa ever since I was a kid. But this trip was after a lapse of nearly 10 years. And what a voyage of (re)discovery it was. We spent an entire half-day exploring, doing much more walking this time than previously, but dont regret it. Although,at certain religious monuments, it took some courage to walk barefoot on the hot sands and stone paving under the noonday sun. As for the museum, I would recommend visiting AFTER the site visit because one is then in a better position to relate to, and appreciate, the artefacts and displays in the museum. This is a large set of sites spread over a large area which needs a car or bike to get around fully. You buy your tickets at the museum and the museum itself is worth a quick look around. The sites near the museum end are the most historically significant - palace etc but least attractive. I.e. Very ruined. As you move to the further away sites they get better to look at high temples and full stupas. The best is last with the 3 carved Buddhas out of a sheer rock face. This is well worth seeing however a couple of warnings This is expensive second only to Siguirya for entrance fee cost Also it has the most hassle from sellers and beggars we encountered in Sri Lanka probably as it is spaced out but flat making access easy. Every car park you are accosted as soon as you exit your car/ coach. It's not aggressive just wearing.

Polonnaruwa ruin site was a good experience. Travel through by bicycle was enjoyable. Many shaded paths. Ruins are in good condition for being over 1000 years old. Some staff were very informative. See Disney movie Monkey Kingdom to learn about the monkeys that live there.

Its amazing to think that a site of this size was built over 1,000 years ago and is breathtaking to see now. We cycled between the buildings, which was much quicker than walking, though hot. You need to cover up in some areas, so take appropriate clothes, and shoes off means walking on very hot stones, so socks might be useful. One of the most fascinating parts of the visit was the bus loads of school kids who found western visitors more interesting than the archaeology, though their open-mouthed stares turned to huge smiles when we smiled at them.

The ancient city is nice to visit but not like a great highlight we thought. Entrance fee and quality don't match with each other. Don't go cycling here, it's so hot. The best memories we have about Polonnaruwa is actually about our stay in the Green guesthouse which was great!

If doesn't mind about sun and heat, rent a bicycle and cycle around the spot. Might be sandy and dusty but it's a great experience and adventurous too! Well, can't compare with Angkor Wat, but different history and a story. Good visit. But price slightly higher as is USD25 per entry.

The ruins are interesting to see but unless you are right into your archeology then it probably isn't going to wow you that much and at $25 entry it's not great value for money. I recommed getting a mode of transport such as tuk tuk or bicycle as it's a big site and also wear socks if you plan on going when the sun is high as walking on hot stones isn't very pleasant if you aren't used to it!

Polonnnarowa is a vast archealogical site with many differing ruins to visit. Luckily you can drive around the old city. It's expensive - Rs 3,350 (Sri Lankan Rupees), roughly SGD$33.50 or US $27.50 per person. It's hot. Like really hot during the day!! Take plenty of water..... It's a long drive from Colombo. Read LONG. May only look 229km but that's Sri Lankan for about 5 hours or so. We travelled from Passikudah on the East Coast on better roads, distance of 72km. That was 2 hours. Interesting, 900 years old and worth a visit. Remember it's hot ! Top tip: stay in Dambulla or nearby and visit Dambulla Cave Temple, Sigiriya Lion Rock and Polonnoruwa together. This will saves hours and hours and hours on the road

Maybe we choose wrong day - it was holiday and there was so many sri lankan people inside with cars, buses, vans... I thought this is an atraction where you can walk between historical buildings but it was more walking around trashes. For turist entrence fee is 25$ so you pay to see something and for sri lankan is ofc for free, like everywhere. Im okay with it, just than I want to see something not sri lankan people leaving trash all around. Really, there are so many better places where you dont need to pay.

Ruins of palaces, ramparts, moats, audience halls, religious edifices, inscriptions in stone, stupas, shrines, ancient meditation centres, images, ponds and rock carvings to name some, are spread out in an area where a traveller can easily spend one day to see them all. A visit to Sri Lanka will not be complete without a visit to Polonnaruwa archaeological sites if a traveller appreciate history and ancient architecture of this island. It has a tale to tell you!

The ruins are absolutely amazing. I went there with my friend from England. For locals it was free entrance and they can enter from anywhere, but for foreigners it was Rs. 3,500 and they had to go to a certain location to get it and enter from another gate.  The management staff could not speak English, wasn't helpful, rude and unpleasant. There were no English signages, no clean toilets or maps given for the foreigners even though they are charged a high amount.  Even though the ruins were nice, the time and hassle is not worth it and the place is not geared for tourists..

If time permits and if you have some interest in the archeological ruins, it is worth to take your time at each site. Each site has its own significance and it is interesting to know some background info from your guide. Most of the temples require you to remove your shoes.

The city of polonnaruwa covers a vast area. We had a guide who showed us the most interesting places and gave us the historical facts. We would have missed so much without him well worth the tip. The reclining Buddha and the other two at the end of our tour were amazing .

This is part of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa & is steeped in history. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site & very well preserved. As with most of these sites in Sri Lanka there is an entrance fee of $25 per head. We went there with an english speaking guide which is helpful if you want to get the most from the visit. There are many different artefacts to see & explore & we both felt it was worth going along to view and get a better understanding of the culture & history.

The best time to visit this place is early morning or late afternoon because the temperature in the mid noon is very high. If you are going to visit this place, I suggest that your get some info about the history of  the heritage before visiting. Otherwise you will be just like looking at the ordinary walls or statues. By right the management board should set up some signboards explaining the history of the heritage in English and Chinese, other than their own language.

Don't miss this place, if you're a lover of history and culture. The museum is worth spending time in, and provides an excellent introduction for exploring the relatively near ruins...you'll still need to hire a tuk tuk or driver for the day though, it's preferable to walking such distances on your own, unless you cycle! Wear shoes and socks, you will have to take off your shoes for many shrines, with hot ground to walk on! I would recommend visiting the Hindu buildings (like the Siva Devales) in addition to the great Buddhist ruins, because they provide a great added perspective of the syncretic nature of ancient Sri Lankan culture. And don't forget that the massive, beautiful lake nearby...is actually a tank made by the greatest of the empire's kings!

An ancient city which was the 2nd largest city in ancient Sri Lanka. Amazing remains of temples and monuments. A garden city complete with water gardens and shrines. Once held the tooth of the Lord Buddha before the fall of the city. Great walking paths with tall, spreading shady trees for coolness. Take plenty of water as there are no taps or shops close. You will need a hat. Respectful clothing expected.

It is very nice to go here by bicycle then you can go closer to the temples. You can see here the old culture and temples of Sri Lanka. But don't forget that there are rules when you want to go in a temple: shoes out, cover you're shoulders and knees. If you like to see the culture and history of Sri Lanka then you must see this.

We took a bus from sigiriya (transfer in Inamaluwa) and it took us about 2h and 200rs (2p) to get to Polonnaruwa. Easy. Never believe tuk tuk drivers that tell you there is no bus or it comes once in an hour.....these are lies. At the busstop in polonnaruwa there are a lot of people who can rent you a bike. We hired a bike for 250rs each. By bike, you can see the entire park in one day, but start early! The park is nice and there are some great remains, but if you compare it to other mayor unesco sites, we were a bit dissapointed (especially after paying so much). They could use the money to place proper descriptions. some of them are very hard to read. In the museum you can find reconstructions of the buildings. Very interesting! Conclusion: we had a nice day, but had higher expectations.

This is the site of the most recent Sri Lankan kingdom after the previous one was destroyed by the cholas from india- those ruins are in Anuradhapura. It is very well preserved with several fine examples of stonework and carving. The remains of the palace that was once seven stories high are amazing. There are Buddhist sculptures and paintings that are a must see. The museum is very well made and detailed. One learns a lot about ancient Sri Lanka.

IT's really mesmerizing archaeological site protected by UNESCO as a heritage historical place. Marvelous piece of architecture, rock carvings, brick buildings, 7 storied brick buildings. Words are not enough to explain. A must see site...

Visit the birtually non air-con museum first to understand what the ruins looked like originally and then compare the ruin once discovered through to excavation. The site covers 5ha so transport of some description is essential as it can be hot, humid and can also rain heavily as we found out. A guide is useful but not essential if you research beforehand. That said, R500-1000 helps the local guides and won't break the bank.  They show you the best places for photos too.

Go early as the heat can be oppressive although there's lots of shady trees. Interesting group of ruins - an ancient city and the ruins are situated in about 4 different locations. Pity about the stray dogs hanging around, a bit off putting

I can't imagine how there could be negative reviews about this place. I found it to be absolutely breathtaking as I adore ruins and history so it's definitely my thing. There's so much to see here so I suggest going as early as you can because as the day goes on it will get very hot. I rented a bicycle, which is a must because it's far too spread out to walk around and there's so much to see. There was monsoon like rain for about half an hour so I hid under a vendors tent and ate short eats so there was no harm done. I suggest bringing a poncho or a rain jacket with you just incase. While I was there I saw many people getting shuttled around on cars and buses. I feel as though you would miss the essence of this place by doing so. But if you have mobility issues it would be the way to go.

From a historical point of view, an absolut must place to visit. The story about the place is very interesting if you have a good guide. But most of the sites are only ruines today- not much to see. The different sites are far from each other and you can rent a bicycle -do not. It is crazy hot, so do the tour in a air-conditioned car (and step out on the sites for a short visit). Allow 2 hours for a visit.

This site began as a kingdom subsequent to the fall of Anaradhapura.  It exists as a well-preserved city where you can see shops, temples, royal housing and ruins of unknown function.  Because it is more intact, it is much more evocative than Anaradhapura (at least for me).  It is pretty humbling to realize that this huge kingdom peaked during the dark ages of Europe.  The kings of Anaradhapura and Polonnaruwa undertook massive water works to ensure the success of agriculture in a regions where monsoons are followed by a dry period.  Polonnaruwa is very photogenic and represents a key period in Sri Lankan history and a neglected facet of Western history.

Polonnaruwa ruins are scattered over an extensive area of about 4km from north to south. You can see everything in a single long day, but start early to do the city justice. You can get there by Tuk Tuk and cycle or walk the ruins. Don't leave belongings in the Tuk Tuk unattended as monkeys destroy, wear and eat whatever they find. Take water, hat, sunblock and thick pair of socks (stones and ground heat up) when you have to remove shoes and mosquito repellent. Polonnaruwa started in the 10th century when the South Indian Chola dynasty had conquered Sri Lanka. It was the thriving commercial and religious centre of Sri Lanka some 800 years ago and is enclosed by three concentric walls and filled with parks and gardens. At the centre of the city lies the royal palace complex (1153 – 1186), including the kings audience hall with beautiful stone carved elephants on the walls, the swimming pool with crocodile mouth spouts.  To the north are the city’s religious buildings. The sacred Quadrangle, contains the finest group of remains in Sri Lanka. The largest monuments are found in the northern part of the city; Menik Vihara, Rankot Vihara, Alahana Pirivena and Jetavana monasteries, including the famous Buddha statues of the Gal Vihara and the soaring Lankatilaka shrine. To the west of the city lies the great artificial lake, the Parakrama Samudra (“Sea of Parakramabahu”), providing a beautiful backdrop to the town – an evening stroll along the waterside Potgul Mawatha makes a scenic way to end a day. The lake was created by the eponymous king, Parakramabahu, though sections of the irrigation system date right back to the third century AD. Covering some 26 square kilometres, the lake provided the medieval city with water, cooling breezes and an additional line of defence, and also irrigated over ninety square kilometres of paddy fields. After a breach in the walls in the late thirteenth century, the tank fell into disrepair, and was restored to its original size only in the 1950s. Although Polonnaruwa doesn’t have the huge religious significance of Anuradhapura, the city’s religious remains are still held sacred and signs outside many of the ruins ask you to remove your shoes as a token of respect – quite painful, unless you’re accustomed to walking barefoot over sharp gravel, while the ruins’ stone floors can often reach oven-like temperatures in the midday sun. So be sure to pack thick socks.

First of all, buy the entrance ticket at the museum (museum is included in the ticket price and it is worthy a visit). Then head for the Polonnaruwa complex, about 15 mins away from the museum (ask for directions). To rent a bicycle is really easy. This was the capital of Sri Lanka at a time when the indigenous Buddhism was being blended with Hinduism.  The Sri Lankan kings arranged marriages for their sons with brides from Hindu kingdoms to the north.  the result is an insight into how cultures interact and compete.  The moonstones at Anuradhapura contain four large animals, elephant, horse, lion and bull.  They were place at entrances of image houses so when people walked over them they were encouraged to contemplate the Buddhist transition from ordinary life of struggle and desire to the inner center of the stone, the lotus, signifying inner peace. The Hindu tradition was completely different.  Stepping on something was considered to defile it.  The cow was sacred, so it came off the Polonnaruwa  moonstones.  But beyond that, the whole act of entering the image house was changed from one of contemplation, to one of reverence.  There is far more here, including helpful recreations of what the palaces and monks quarters may have looked like.  Still, like Anuradhapura, most of Polonnaruwa is still buried in the ground.  what a great  opportunity for an eager young archeologist.

Polonnaruwa is the second ancient capital (12th century) of Sri Lanka. It is a large area with ruins of the ancient city: city walls, palaces, monasteries, stupas, temples. You could easily do a quick tour of the main sites in a couple of hours, but I would recommend to take more time, like 4-6 hours. If you are not interested in history, or cannot mentally bring ruins to life, this may not be your thing. Start with the museum, which is small and simple, but does a good job of introducing the site, with explanation of the history, and for all the main buildings an explanation of their use, pictures of how they were found by archeologists and models of their original appearance. Then work your way north, through the various groupings of buildings. The not-to-be-missed ones are (1) the royal palace and audience hall, (2) the quadrangle area with the Vatadage (a circular building thought to have been the place where they kept the tooth relic was kept), (3) the Lankatilaka temple, with the remains of a large brick buddha statue, and the adjacent white stupa, and (4) Gal Vihara, a series of four Buddha statues cut from the same large rock. As a bonus, go visit the small but excellent lotus pool. Apparently early July is not yet the tourist season, and therefore we did not experience the crowds that apparently usually swarm the place. Instead we saw a limited number of tourists, and several school groups in white uniforms. Practical tips: - Transport is essential, as the sites are too far apart to walk, especially in the July heat. There are tuktuks and you may have a car. We opted for bicycles and were very happy with that choice. It gives a good human sense of the distances, the roads are good, flat and safe, and there is enough shade. - take lots of water - many of the buildings are considered holy, and you will need to take of shoes and hats. Shoulders and legs must be covered. White dress is considered most respectful. I would recommend taking slippers (everybody else does). Note that the sand and stone floors can get very hot and we saw some people with painful burns on their footsoles. You may want to take socks. - there are souvenir salesmen and people offering guide services everywhere. Be firm in your 'no thank yous' otherwise they may negatively affect your mood.

This is where most tourists are and this is what most guides show. But what impressed me most of all was the outer city. Dozens and dozens of basements of the houses, incredible Lankathilaka, terraced pools, and much less people than in the central part make it so much more atmospheric, authentic, and quiet. A visit to Polonnaruwa takes time and energy.  We are talking about a small city here and there a large number of individual areas to see.  To 'do' the lot would take days and, unless you are an archaeologist, you would almost certainly be 'ruined out' by the end of the first day. Most people therefore go for the main attractions like The Quadrangle, Shiva Devale, Gal Vihara, Vatadage,the Royal Palace Group, Island Garden and Lankatilaka.  Even to do these, you will need transport and at the very least 5-6 hours which, in the temperatures (30-33C) existing for most of the year, is seriously debilitating. However, it is worth the effort as the ruins are all impressive, though they do require a certain degree of imagination to conceive of the sheer magnitude of the whole site and the manpower that must have been required to build it. Polonnaruwa is a must for any visitor to Sri Lanka and fully repays the exertion expended.

Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka’s splendid medieval capital was established as the first city of the land in the 11th Century, A.D. It replaced Anuradhapura, which was plundered, made desolate and laid hopelessly bare to the invading armies from South India. Three Kings dominate the chronicles of the city and the period. The city reached a dazzling but pitifully brief zenith in the 12th century and though ravaged by invasion in the centuries that followed, much evidence remains of the old grandeur and glory.The ruins of the ancient city stand on the east shore of a large artificial lake, the Topa Wewa Lake, or Parakrama Samudraya (the Sea of Parakrama), built by King Parakramabahu I (1153-86), whose reign was Polonnaruwa‘s golden age. Within a rectangle of city walls stand palace buildings and clusters of dozens of dagobas, temples and various other religious buildings.A scattering of other historic buildings can be found to the north of the main complex, outside the city walls and close to the main road to Habarana and Dambulla. To see many of the relics excavated from the site such as the stone lion which once guarded the palace of King Nissanka Malla, or the fine Hindu bronzes unearthed from the ruins of the Siva Devale Temple – you may have to visit the National Museum in Colombo, where they are kept. However, with the opening of the new Polonnaruwa Visitor Information Centre and its museum in 1998/9 some of the key exhibits were scheduled to return to the place where they were discovered.

Sri Lanka's history is going back to 543 BC. The first kingdom was made in the 4th century BC, which lasted until the 10th century AD. King Wijayabahu the 1st rescued from the South Indian Invaders and made it the capital of the country. There are another two important kings who ruled Polonnaruwa. King Parakramabahu (1153-1186) and King Nissankamalla (1187-1196). There are endless amount of ruins in Polonnaruwa belong to 11-13 century AD, made by these important kings. It is also a world heritage site declared by the UNESCO. There are so many ruins of the palaces, monasteries, temples, image houses, ponds, arms halls, pleasure gardens etc. King Parakramabahu's Statue, Parakrama Samudra, (Ocean), Tooth relic quadrangle  Lankathilaka or Dot of Sri Lanka, Northern temple or Stone temple, Milky stupa, Rankoth vehera, Lotus pond are some of the major attractions in Polonnaruwa. Polonnaruva was an ancient capital city of Sri lanka up until about 800 years ago. These are the ruins of an area that was ruled over by many kings over some 300 years. It was declared a world heritage site in 1982. The area is enormous and contains fantastic ruins in a well maintained area that is a pleasure to stroll through. Walking would take forever so I strongly recommend hiring a bike (available near entrance) to move between different areas. We spent about 3 hours, with bike and being dropped at one end and picked up at the other. You would have no trouble filling a day in here. Nothing is fully intact but what remains provides a wonderful example of what existed here. There are some large palace buildings, reception rooms of various kings, many temples and places of worship, man made pools and ponds as part of an intricate ancient water system. I spent about 4 hours touring the archeological park. There were signs all around and the bicycle place also gave me a map so I had no trouble navigating the park. Most of the ancient ruin sites had information in English. Of course, having a guide (easily available for a fee around the sites) would help but I opted not to have a guide. The weather was very very hot so please make sure to hydrate yourself. I had 2 coconuts in the span of 4 hours. During the time I was there, there weren't too many tourists so I got pretty good photos and also enjoyed just sitting in the shade and looking at the magnificent ruins. There were also some restoration works going on and the park itself was very well-maintained with minimal trash and comfortable pavements to ride on. That made me realize that the entrance fees are completely necessary to maintain this place. If we could travel thousands of kilometers to visit this country, what's a few bucks to contribute to the upkeep of the site. How else would we be able to see the magnificence of this park in a comfortable state? This is one of those things that you must do during your visit to Sri Lanka. Like some others here, you're going to be disappointed if you have already been to Angkor etc. Since most of the structures here are very ancient and were wooden, all that really remains are the stone supports. LOOK OUT for two things: first, the site is very spread out, and in that heat you would be crazy not to rent a bike at the front entrance (500 RS). Second, you have to have your shoes off for the structures in the so-called Quadrangle (as with most other SL temples), and this is tightly monitored by fellows who seem to greatly enjoy their job. Firstly, you really need a guide to get the best from the visit. We were travelling for a week and our driver took us around the various sites and told us about the history and significance of each location. Make sure you start at the museum. Here you will pick up your ticket that will be needed across the vast site to get access to the various areas. The museum shows some models that recreate what the site would have looked like originally, as well as showing some of the smaller artefacts that have been discover over the last 100 or so years. You have to remember that this isn't a huge vast museum with lots of money and resources like those you may see in other countries. It is more like we would expect perhaps from a temporary exhibit, but nonetheless lots of information. As I said, the site itself is vast, and it can take a 10min drive to move between the various significant sites, but on your way you will go past other smaller areas. If you are very interest in the history and archaeology then it would be easy to spend a couple of dates exploring, but for most a few hours would suffice. It is quite funny reading reviews of people saying that may of the sites are in ruins, or that they were in a poor state. This is a site that is around 1000 years old! I'd argue it was in pretty good nick. And as for complaints of the admission price the $25 equivalent fee is nothing and surely helps to keep the place in the condition it is in. We visited early in the morning, which I would recommend. As the day moved on the heat became almost unbearable and water is a necessity. Although the sites are historical, the ruins of the temples are still considered holy, so if you wish to walk amongst the ruins then you have to take your shoes off at the entrance and make sure that your shoulders, chest and knees are covered up. This doesn't mean the whole location, literally just the ruins of the temples. There were a lot of people selling postcards and trinkets around the area, particularly in the car parks. A polite 'no thank you' usually sees them on their way, though it can take a couple of goes. A few of the people who were selling seemed to be disabled  and it was quite hard at times knowing that we are much more fortunate and well-off than they are. The small cost of buying a set of postcards is virtually nothing to us, so if you plan on sending one back home I would urge you to take the time buy a few from these people and offer a little back.

The ruins of ancient Sri Lankan capital are magnificent and extensive. Though some visitors complain that there is nothing to see there if you have seen some grand ruins of SE Asia, I cannot agree. Every country has its own history and atmosphere, you just have to look and listen if you have at least minimum interest in the country and its history and not just „ticking off“ the visited places. We were amazed at the extent, the individual structures and the infrastructure linking all of the Polonnaruwa sites.  We were also somewhat amazed that we were able to walk on so many of the structures (with shoes off).  Given the important cultural nature of this site make sure that you dress appropriately. The Polonnaruwa musuem is outstanding for its content and clear explanation of the history of the area. You can easily spend a full day at Polonnaruwa. Visit the museum first.

Polonnaruwa's ruins are closer to each other than Anuradhapura's. However, its best to have some sort of transportation as there is a lot to see. we had bicycles and it was perhaps the most perfect way to see the sites. The famous sites are filled with tourists and schoolkids, but its not difficult to find sites that nobody seems to be visiting. The stupas offer no shade, so its good to have on some sunscreen/hats. A day in Pollonaruwa was a memorable one. I would give this a better rating if the ticket price was more appropriate. In my opinion a top end ticket price for the old city of Polonnaruwa would be 1000 Rupees. That's in comparison to other sites around Sri Lanka and other sites in Asia such as the Angkor Kingdom in Cambodia. 3000 rupees is incredibly overpriced. We spent half a day cycling around Polonnaruwa. There is plenty to see both in terms of ruined sites and religious temples. It felt somewhat strange especially with a almost bacchanalian girl performing a whirling dervish type dance around the temple. Make sure you bring your own guide book; as with many other historical places in Sri Lanka, maps of the site and information can be lacking. Even if the entrance to here and many other places are steep, these places have to be visited as they are magnificent historical monuments and I personally think subsidising local tourism is good.

Really is a must visit on your tour or visit of Sri Lanka. This area encompasses the vastness of the old 12th century capital. Some buildings are better preserved than others but lets face facts, these buildings are 800-900 years old. Lots of ancient architecture in the form of monasteries and buddhist temples. Can't quite remember the price but i do remember thinking it was quite expensive. However, where else do you get to see such history and ancient Sri Lankan architecture? Bring a bottle of water for the walk around as you will need it! I fortunately was travelling with a guide and car which cut out the need for a backpack and the long(ish) walk to each of the different sites. Remember it does get very hot in Sri Lanka. Early morning or late afternoon would be the ideal times to walk around. I never had the luxury of choosing the time to visit as i had an itinerary and so had a make do with tan lines. A very trivial thing but no one likes tan lines!

In my opinion this is worthwhile only if you have a genuine interest in the history of Sri Lanka. It doesn’t have the spectacle value of Sigiriya or the cave temple at Dambulla, and with an entry fee of 3,250 rupees is over-priced. What you actually see is a series of pretty dilapidated ruins dating from about the same period as the Normal churches and cathedrals in England, but while those have been well maintained and preserved these are largely brick and stone bases with pillars standing up here and there. Some large stuppas have more or less survived and there are three or four attractive Buddha statues, but the place has about it a theme park atmosphere, with uniformed attendants telling you to take your shoes off, cover your shoulders and legs etc. (because the temple ruins are still treated as temples), hawkers hassling you to buy carved figures and other tourist merchandise, stallholders offering fruit, drinks and more tourist merchandise, and the drone of  guides reciting material they have memorized from the guide books featuring litanies of the unpronounceable names of kings and their consorts and associates. It all has the feel of a big commercial jamboree with very little soul or atmosphere. The bit I enjoyed most was watching the monkeys attempting to steal the fruit from the stalls or following tourists around in the hope of titbits. If you go I would suggest you don’t take a tour or give in to the sales-talk of tuc-tuc drivers, but hire a bicycle and see the area at your own pace. If you do buy a tour, make sure that the guide actually knows what he’s talking about and also that the price quoted includes that exorbitant park entrance fee. The museum is worth a visit and more modestly priced, and unless you feel like a day in the country among the monkeys and the souvenir vendors is perhaps enough for the casual visitor. The high entry price charged for this and other Sri Lankan attractions means that the backpacker kind of traveller has used up his or her budget for the day just in the entry fee and will be disinclined to make a donation to individual temples, which is a pity, as there might be a lesser risk of the money ending up in some government official's Swiss bank account.The big bucks of course don't apply to Sri Lankans, who are allowed to look at things for free.  As soon as you see entry prices quoted in American dollars you know you're in trouble. It also produces an unpleasant atmosphere where anyone of the wrong colour is stopped by a man in a uniform and required to produce a pass. Why does that make me think of South Africa? Comment from Jean, David's partner  – I largely agree but you do have to use a bit of imagination to think what it would have been like living in those days. Actually, excluding present day technology [fancy phones, vehicles] I don’t think it would have been much different. Poor people sweating out hard lives and vast amounts of time, work and money going into religious monuments – what’s differen?. What would Buddha have thought? Personally, I think Buddhism teaches some good attitudes but Buddha himself spent his life sitting under a tree – not very useful in my opinion.

This is both a cultural and historic site. It is the second capital, albeit short lived, after Anuradhapura. Be warned, it is been visited using some form of transport as the sites are scattered along a long road. The best place to start is the museum which houses not only the main finds but also excellent models. It also has photographs presenting both "before and after" excavation and restoration. I would recommend going early and spending at least one hour. Our guide/driver commenced with the statue of Parakramabahu I who was the driving force behind the construction of the immense man-made lake. There is also another small temple close to the statue. The main sites occupy a long stretch of road elsewhere. The sites are grouped into secular and religious. The Inner Citadel hosts the palace, council chamber and royal baths. Further on is what may be deemed the heart of the overall complex with the Quadrangle. Here are a number of Buddhist temples including two former resting places of the Tooth relic. The Vatadage is particularly noteworthy being of unusual design and housing for Buddha statues facing out at the cardinal points. Moving along the road are the Rankot Vihara and Lankatilaka which are both impressive in their own right. The Gal Vihara is arguably the highlight of the entire site and this has a separate entry. Finishing off is the lotus pool, a beautifully carved stepped construction in the shape of the flower. Also the Tivanka Patamaghara, both of which formed part of a monastery Do take water, do take a long time, do have a guide and ignore the pedlars (politely of course). If you don't like history don't go.

The city was established by the Tamil Chola after their invasion and occupation of Sri Lanka in 993 AD. They were defeated and pushed out of the city about 50 years later by the Singhala King Vijayabahu. The ruins bear witness to the city’s Hindu and Buddhist heritage.  However the majority of the ruins date from the mid 12th century reign of the great Parakramabahu I (1153-86). Highlights that should not be missed include the: •	massive brick Lankatilaka and a huge image of Buddha; •	Gal Vihara, with its majestic group of four Buddha statues carved out of a rock wall: •	Tivanka Pilimage, with wall paintings illustrating the previous lives of Buddha: •	Quadarnagle collection of buildings including relic houses; •	Shiva Devalaya Hindu temple •	Rangot Dagoba outside the quadrangle •	Royal palace and the queens bathing pool; and •	Council Chambers The city and the northern dry-zones was finally abandoned by the Singhalese kings in the 14th century. At a rather hefty $25 a head entrance fee this is not a cheap outing. So make the most of it and give yourself 3-4 hours, wear good shoes and a hat but you have to remove both at certain locations.

A place steeped on history. U must have a good guide to explain the ruins. Beware of the numerous souvenir sellers who can be pests. Don t miss the lotus pond and do bring sunglasses and bottles of water , a hat and a good pir of shoes.

Guidebook/Map Available, Photos Prohibited in Visitor Center Exhibits, Tour by Car During Hot Weather, Take socks Polonnaruwa is a huge archeological site rich in cultural history of Sri Lanka dating from 900 years ago.  I toured the grounds with my driver in early May and spent about four hours at the many, many different sites starting from the Visitor’s Center (then to the Palace ruins, Sacred Quadrangle, Golden Pinnacle Stupa, etc., all listed in the guidebook – see attached photo). Having toured the grounds during the hot season, I could not imagine taking a bicycle or walking around the grounds with the pervasive heat.  Having a car and driver allowed me to spend more time studying the sites, taking photos and less time travelling from one point to the other.  Distances between major sites seemed large.  From the southernmost point (the king’s statue) to the northernmost point (the Tivanka image house) is about four kilometers. While touring the grounds, I reminded myself that Polonnaruwa was once a thriving capital city and can only imagine it’s former grandeur.  The visitor’s center/museum was extremely informative with the hypothetical architectural models of the palace, temples and audience hall, now only extant as ruins. I would recommend tourists to not miss studying these models before seeing the ruins (see attached photo). Other tips: --Take socks.  When entering some of the temples (e.g. Vatage), visitors are expected to take off their shoes observing respect to the hallowed grounds.  During hot weather, the stone tiles are like surface of a grill.  Wearing sock could definitely mitigate the discomfort. --Purchase the guidebook published by the Central Cultural Fund. The pictures suggest that the book was written probably two decades ago, but the information (and map of each important site) is still highly relevant.  I purchased a copy at the small bookshop at the back of the visitor’s center/museum, near the toilets.  I’ve also seen the guidebook for sale at the Sigiriya museum bookshop. --Photography is prohibited at the exhibits in the visitor’s center. --Watch out for packs of simians at the palace ruins.  Some can be quite aggressive.  One tried to snatch my camera from my hands.

The place is vast; if you have a motorbike you can purchase a half-day ticket and finish it in half a day. If you're on the bicycle or walking, then you'll need the full day tix. After several days heavy rain and poor visibility, it was hot and sunny again the day we went round Polonnaruwa.  It was a beautiful drive from Dambulla, going around the Minneriya tank and through the park, and our experienced driver/guide ensured we saw the ruins to best advantage, starting with the excellent museum.  This really helped to put the site in context, as it is huge - far bigger than I had imagined.  He took us from place to place by car, and we took his advice as to the order in which to do it. Bear in mind that many of the stupa and temple ruins are still regarded as holy sites and the usual rules about removing hats & footwear obtain - it really helps to have easily removable shoes! If you only had 1 of the 2 ancient cities to visit in Sri Lanka, between Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, I would say that the latter is a better option. Compared to Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa has a greater variety of things to see, in the form of temples, statues, domes, a citadel, throne and other religious structures (or their remains/ruins). As they are ancient cities, the state of Polonnaruwa also fits the title more aptly. However, what I didn't like with this place was the lack of ease you could navigate around and outside the place. We visited Polonnaruwa in December and enjoyed a full day exploring this huge site. You need to keep your driver with you to ferry you from one area to another. There are so many palaces, temples, buddhas; some virtually intact, others in ruins or being restored. There are lots of little stalls selling drinks and snacks dotted about, but if you want lunch you have to leave and then come back in. Knees and shoulders should be covered for the temples and buddhas. I loved the reclining buddha in particular, it really is stunning. We came across a group of monkeys cooling off and playing in a lake which was so entertaining to watch, a real treat. A beautiful day to remember.

The polonnaruwa ruins are definitely impressive and better intact than the Anuradhapura ruins. Anuradhapura requires more imagination but the size of the grounds gives a hint at what an enormous gathering of monks it must have been. Polonnaruwa is smaller but has more (half) surviving buildings and you don't need so much imagination. A full day, preferably by car, is required to see all the sights. But the main ones are grouped closely together and can be seen in half a day too. Some of the central ruins are delicately decorated with sculptures and much still remains of the original building. A bit more far out we really liked the Thivanka image house, where the walls are still decorated with the original plaster and frescoes. Also the Gal Vihara is unbelievable beautiful. We went to see both Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa and we don't regret doing both since we had plenty of time. If you are pressed for time, and have to choose, we would recommend seeing Polonnaruwa.

Polonnaruwa was a fascinating visit to the 11th-12th Century former capital city, on the banks of a reservoir of the same age. We started at the museum, which itself is pretty huge and full of artifacts from the site, and describes all the structures you'll see around the city itself!  You could spend hours in here if you wanted to look at everything, so we ended up skipping to the most interesting bits and managed to get through in half an hour or so. When we came out there were hawkers following us round trying to sell us souvenirs - they were quite desperate as it was the quiet season, and the price for a stone Ganesha statue rapidly dropped as I kept saying no thanks! The City itself is full of amazing sights with temples, palaces, ornate swimming pools, the huge stupa, lotus pool, the rock temple with the Huge stone Buddhas carved into the face of a huge granite rock face, to mention just a few. The carving on the buildings is amazing and the moonstones still in place are fantastic (I am surprised you can still walk through and on a lot of the site. The downsides were the disfigured beggars following us round shouting 'you give me money' and hawkers trying to sell us rubbish souvenirs and sun-hats constantly.  It didn't ruin the whole experience, but it did take some of the shine off it for us.  I guess if it was busier they would have spread themselves around, but there were very few visitors at the time so they followed us relentlessly.

Thoroughly disrespectful. The recumbent Buddha was another highlight. All in all a great outing for three to four hours even with a teenager!
