"Polonnaruwa The Medieval capital of Sri Lanka" The history of early Sri Lanka was very carefully recorded and written down by monks. The Mahavamsa (Great Chronicle) records the earlier period of the Sri Lankan, and Chulavamsa (lesser Chronicle), gives an accurate picture of the 'Polonnaruwa' period. King Vijayabahu I In 1070 AD the Sinhala King Vijayabahu I liberated the country by defeating the Cholas, and kept Polonnaruwa as his capital. Vijayabahu succeeded in repairing much of the irrigation system in the island, encouraged trade and brought some prosperity back to the country. King Parakramabahu I King Parakramabahu I (1153-86) raised Polonnaruwa to its heights. He erected huge buildings, drained swamps and planted vast areas with crops, planned beautiful parks, created wildlife sanctuaries, restored earlier monuments & even undertook military expeditions against Burma and India. However his crowning achievements were the creation of the 2400 hectare tank (about 15 Km2), so large it was named the Parakrama Samudra (Sea of Parakrama); and the unification of the three orders of monks, the Maha vihara, Jetavana and Abhayagiri into one Sangha or 'Supreme Order of Monks'. The greatness of his achievement was to ensure the survival of Buddhism in the dark centuries ahead. Parakramabahu was the last great king of Sri Lanka. King Nissankamalla King Nissankamalla (1187 - 96), although claimed himself to be a great builder, was not. And squandered most of the country's wealth trying to match his predecessor's deeds.

We had a half day in Polonnaruwa before our full day doing the all paid sights, so we hired bicycles from our hotel to explore. We wanted to do as much as we could without our ticket so we could concentrate on those sights the next day. First we visited the "rest house group" immediately behind the archaeological museum. You need your ticket to visit the museum, but you don't need it to see these ruins. There is a well-preserved stone lion here set in tall trees overlooking the lake. We cycled north, eventually coming out on the main road. We decided to try to reach the "summer house ruins" which you can see from the rest house group. This involved cycling along the busy road, past the turn-off for the northern monuments (for which you need your ticket) around a bend and then we took the first street to the left. There were no signs in English. This was a quiet street that was much more pleasant to cycle on and at the end of it (impossible to miss) was the track across the lake to the ruins. Just note we did this in the dry season, so the lake was all grass here, but I think it must be possible even in the wet season. Cycling on the grassy lake was wonderful - we were the only people there and the scale of the lake is just so huge. The ruins are uninteresting once you get there, but we decided to return via the lake rather than by the road. We were able to cycle all the way back to the rest house area where we started across the lake. Saw lapwings and lots of cows which mostly just ignored us. Very cool! Once back on the city streets we decided to cycle South along the Bund road. This is very scenic - in both directions and we saw lots of Brahminy Kites fishing. We went all the way to the "Southern Group" which also does not require a ticket. There is a large statue of King Parakramabahu  and some other ruins in which we enjoyed walking around. Finally we returned back along the bund and stopped (along with lots of locals) to watch an amazing sunset. The next day we bought our site ticket and we hired bikes again and spent the whole day with a rest in the middle doing all the remaining sites with our day ticket. We got to the observatory just after 8am and it was quiet and peaceful. We found the bikes invaluable and were able to cycle to the northern group INSIDE the park so we didn't need to go out onto the main road again. We had a great two days here.

Since this was a capital city for some time there is a number of tooth temples also present, however most of them are quite in bad state. All in all I would definitely recommend visit of this site, just keep your mind open and try to use imagination.

Polonnaruwa is an extraordinary archaeological site which far exceeds anything I expected to see in Sri Lanka. Dating from the Middle Ages, it offers an extraordinary collection of structures, most of them beautifully preserved. The level of detail on these buildings is extraordinary. Every railing, staircase, terrace and sculpture has been exquisitely carved, making this one of the most photogenic of historic sites. We particularly liked the lustrous moonstones which had been placed before every staircase. The site is also very large so allow yourself several hours to walk around here. Don't miss the magnificent Reclining Buddha carved into a rock face; this makes the ideal end point for a journey around this lush, shady site. The entrance fee is not cheap, but we did not mind paying it once we had seen what was on offer.

Gal Vihara (Sinhala: stone temple), Buddhist Temple at (UNESCO World Heritage Site) at Polonnaruwa, Sri Lanka is the most perfect specimen of Buddha statue hewn out of solid stone. Crafted during the reign of King Parakrabahu (1153-1186 A.C), Gal Vihara statues are still in complete preservation with their irresistible charm and sublimity. It is undeniable that the sculptors of Gal Vihara were of greater skill and expertise in the art of stone sculpture in Sri Lanka. The images at Gal Vihara have brought about higher level of awakening in the observers with respect of Buddhist art in Sri Lanka. Gal Vihara, Polonnaruwa known as “The Northern Temple” in the beginning of its history, is a cave complex, about 27 meters in length and 10 meters in height at the centre and sloping towards the ends, with sculptures carved on the solid rock in four shrines. Gal Vihara, like numerous other Buddhist shrines of Sri Lanka, is a shrine of Theravada Buddhism. Then again Gal Vihara testifies to the influence of Mahayana Buddhism during the 12th century. Caves of Gal Vihara Gal Vihara consists of four cave shrines with sculptures hallowed out of a granite rock.Caves from left to right are (a) Cave of Vijjadharas, (b) Excavated Cave, (c) Cave of Standing Image and (d) Cave of Reclining Image. Between the Excavated Cave and the Cave of Standing Image is an inscription. In front of the Excavated Cave are remains of a pavilion. Though the brick walls of the four shrines had collapsed centuries ago, the foundations remain giving evidence that each statue was separated from one another.

Expect to spend quite a few hours at the site.  The recumbent Buddha is very impressive - don't leave without seeing it.  It gets hot - although there is more shade here than at other similar sites in Sri Lanka.  Take water, comfortable shoes, and something to shade your head!

Our party was all Asian history and religion buffs; we loved the ruins and the surrounding park.  We had a van and driver, so getting around was easy--and there was always a bottle of water in the van when needed. We arrived early in the morning (highly recommended for all the ancient sites in Sri Lanka), and took over 4 hours to see the ruins inside the ancient city walls near the Parakrama Samudra reservoir which supported the population, and the historic buildings outside the main site (Gal Viharaya's colossal Buddha images, the Lotus Bath, and the Tivanka Pilimage (Gallery of Images), now being repaired, was our last stop before visiting the museum, and well worth seeing, although few visitors make it to the Gallery.  Very fine ancient temple murals cover the interior walls, and a rich variety of frescoes decorate the exterior.) Beautiful, well-reconstructed and well-maintained.  The links to Thervada Buddhism in mainland Southeast Asia interested us (e.g., Satmahal Prasada, which strongly resembles an ancient chedi about 30 km. from where we live in Northern Thailand), as well as the advanced knowledge of water storage and control which enabled a relatively large population to live there.

The downside first: As with all Sri Lankan sites and attractions, the entrance fees are quite high for foreign tourist  - we are not to sure about the money being used for the upkeep of the place. (And as with all places in Sri Lanka, bathroom facilities are limited, even though you pay US$ 25 to get in.) But the visit is a must if you want to understand Sri Lanka and its culture, history and development. Start at the museum, get some transport (car or tuk-tuk), as walking is not an option due to the size of this place - and the heat. There is much to see, even though only a small percentage of the area has been excavated. Expect to spend three to five hours if you want to get to know Polonnaruwa. The small CD-rom you get in your ticket is quite useful and a nice souvenir.

A two hour drive from Sigiriya or Anuradhapura, brings you to the historic city of Polonnaruwa. You need about 3 hours to visit this place, and pay a 25 USD ticket and you get a small CDROM also in your ticket. The best way is to hire a tuktuk as it is too hot to do it by foot.

Polonnaruwa, one of Sri Lanka's ancient capitals, is well worth a visit. Polonnaruwa is much more interesting than Anuradhapura (the other ancient capital) as it features a diversity of ruins and monuments rather than stupa after stupa. Of particular interest is the Quadrangle, a compact group of fascinating and diverse ruins in a raised-up area bounded by a wall. The Lankatikala, a cathedral-like building with a huge standing headless Buddha is as fascinating as the Gal Vihara - several Buddha images carved out of a rock. Unfortunately, there is no decent accomodation in Polonnaruwa so you have to base yourself out of Habarana, Sigiriya and Dambulla, a good 1 hours drive away from Polonnaruwa.

The second capital of Sri Lanka between the 11th & 12th centuries AD, Polonnaruwa has a vast number of places to see. I would advice all visitors to try and see the following places of interest: Citadel and Palace Complex: This area consists of the 12th century Palace and Council Chamber of Parakramabahu I, as well as a royal bathing pool (Kumara Pokuna) and changing pavilion. The Quadrangle: Set within an enclosure wall with formalised entrances, the Quadrangle features numerous image houses/shrines, which date from the 11th & 12th centuries AD. The best preserved are the circular relic house known as the Vatadage, and the Thuparama Gedige. Another interesting building is the structure known as Satmahal Prasada, which has an unusual stepped form. Gal Vihara: Is a large rock-cut monastery, which features a large seated image of Buddha, a reclining Buddha, a standing image of Buddha, and an cavernous shrine room. Potgul Vihara: This area was a monastery in the 12th century AD. The attractions are a sculptured figure of King Parakramabahu I or sage Pulasti, and the main monument of the library for sacred book that surmounts a central square terrace and is surrounded by four small solid stupas. Other places of interest include a Rest House visited by the UK monarch Queen Elizabeth II, Lake Parakrama Samudra, and  numerous Hindu shrines.
